SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, there is a matter which very seriously

i
affects the salmon canning Industry of British Columbia to which I would wish to direct the attention of the government. Of course, as we know, the canning industry of my province is one of the most important industries on the Pacific coast. I express my regret incidentally that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) is not in his seat this morning. However, X would ask the Minister of Finance, who is now leading the House, to call the attention of tlie Fisheries Department to the matter which X am about to mention, and to urge upon the minister immediate action in the line which is indicated by the following telegram, which I received from the Canners' Association of British Columbia :
Vancouver, B.C., 26th.
Thos. Earle, M.P.,
Ottawa.
Following message sent to-day to Hon. R. Prefontaine. The Fraser River Canners' Association, in view of the lamentable short run of sockeyes on the Fraser river and the entire absence of salmon from the spawning grounds, respectfully pray that your department will prohibit all fishing on the Fraser river_ from August 29 to September 12 inclusive, in 'order that the balance of sockeyes remaining outside may be enabled to reach the spawning grounds, and the hatcheries get some supply of spawn. If close season not ordered future of industry seriously threatened. Immediate consideration and favourable reply by wire is earnestly requested in the interests of the canners and fishermen. Your energetic support most earnestly requested.
When we find that last year the output of salmon was not much over one-half what it was the previous year, and that this year it is scarcely one-third of last year, it is evident that there is reason for the canners becoming very greatly alarmed that the Fraser river may be depleted of its fish. The canners make the request contained in the telegram in the hope that if their prayer is granted the fish will have an opportunity of getting up to the spawning grounds, and thus the supply of fish maintained by increased opportunities for breeding. This is becoming a necessity to the existence of the industry. I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the Finance Minister, who now leads the House, to the matter, and I ask him to bring it before the proper department with a recommendation that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should see his way clear to grant this request for a close season, which I believe to be in the interest of the salmon industry of British Columbia. If there is anything in the idea these gentlemen have in regard to tlie breeding of the salmon, it certainly will be in the interest of the industry to grant tliis protection, and it can, at ail events, do no liarm, because it will indict no injury upon any class of the community.
Mr. It. I,. BORDEN (Halifax). Slight I be permitted to say a word in connection
with the same matter. A telegram of the same purport as that read by my hon. friend (Sir. Earle) has been placed in my hands, and I have ibeen asked to draw the attention of the government to the matter. This telegram is very much on the same lines as the telegram received by my hon. friend from Victoria (Sir. Earle), and it reads as follows ;
Vancouver, B.C., August 27,1903.
Fraser River Canners' Association have petitioned department for close season from 29th instant to September 12 inclusive. Situation here extremely critical, as I can certify. Fu-lure of industry absolutely threatened, as no salmon have yet reached spawning ground and the run is practically over. Act'with British Columbia members and senators, urging upon the 'department imperative necessity of prompt action. A few days now may save the industry.
This telegram was handed to me by my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter) to-day, as he was obliged to leave to catch a train, and it is at his request that I bring it to the attention of the government. If the situation is as disclosed in the telegram, then the Minister of Finance, who is leading the House will no doubt admit that it should demand the immediate and earnest consideration of the government.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I shall call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the matter. I assume, from the terms of the telegraip, that the subject has already been communicated to the (department, and I have no doubt that It is engaging the attention of the minister.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I think it is very reprehensible indeed that bon. gentlemen should, as it were, get hysterical over a matter of this kind. My hon. friend from Victoria has read one telegram, as has also the leader of the opposition, from the same parties.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: It would appear as if there were going to be a discussion oh this question, and there is no motion before the House.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I shall conclude my remarks, Sir, with the usual motion to adjourn. The hon. member for Victoria has read one telegram which only gives one side of the case. It Is only from one concern interested in this vast and important industry In the province of British Columbia, and it asks that all fishing operations shall cease because, in their opinion, there are no fish getting to the spawning ground. That is a matter which is almost impossible to determine, because the fish, in any event, cannot and do not get to the spawning ground until some time in the fall.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Morrison) has stated that these telegrams are from the same person. They are not from the same person.	.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I understood they contained almost precisely the same wording.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: They are not from the same person. I said that the telegram which I had in my hand was along the same lines as the one read by the hon. member (Mr. Earle), but they are not from the same person at all.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: From whom did the telegrams come ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Mine is from the secretary of the Canners' Association, Mr. Burdis.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: May I ask from whom the other telegram comes ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: There is not the slightest objection ; it is from Mr. Charles Coi-by.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I do not know who Mr. Corby is, and from my knowledge of that industry in British Columbia, I do not know any one of the name engaged in it. We have all received these telegrams from the British Columbia Canners' Association asking that the fishing be prohibited, which means that there shall toe a total suspension of this vast and important industry for a month or so, on the assumption that the fish are not getting to the spawning grounds. Nobody can possibly determine that, because the fish never get to the spawning grounds till the fall, or in a month or two hence ; and although according to these despatches the salmon are not at the present time running in such large quantities as usual, at the same time I have despatches from very reputable people which go to show that the fish are running. For instance, on the 26th of August, the day before these other telegrams were sent, Mr. James Anderson, of the St. Mungo Cannery, on the Fraser river, wires that the salmon are running decidedly good, and that it would be unfair if the department should stop tlie fishing on the Fraser river. We have not heard yet from the fishermen, men who are also affected largely by this. As a representative of the constituency in which the fishing industry is engaged, I have great concern for that industry, but at the same time I think it would be very reprehensible indeed on the part of the department to take cognizance of a despatch which comes from one source alone, however reputable that may be. I may say that there are despatches the other way showing that the fish are running, and that is the statement of the fishermen, who are the people most interested in this matter. I think myself that the department should hesitate, in fact, so far as I am personally concerned, I would urge upon the department not to take any step until they had absolute confirmation of the statement contained in the telegram, and even then I think it would not be a proper policy to suspend fishing. Why should they do so ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
In my opinion, the department should lend a deaf ear to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Victoria, as well as the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition. There is no material before the minister to warrant him in taking any such step at all. If there is any doubt ; if there is a conflict of evidence as to whether the fish are running or not, then the proper course for the department to take is to let the matter alone, and it will adjust itself. I move the adjournment of the House.
Mr. JOHN CHARLTON (North Norfolk), When I was in British Columbia a short time ago, I made some inquiries into the important salmon fishing industry of the Fraser river. I notice that these telegrams state that there is a very marked diminution in the quantity of salmon caught : that the catch last year was very much less than that of the preceding year, and that the catch this year is very much less than last year. My hon. friend from Westminster (Mr. Morrison) takes objection to the statement placed before the House, and says that it emanates only from the canners. Well, I suppose that the canners, having a large investment there, are more deeply interested than any other class of persons engaged in the business. It seems to me, from a knowledge of the way that nets are placed on the Fraser river, that it "would be utterly impossible for salmon to get up the stream.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: That is nonsense.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Perhaps it is nonsense, but at all events the river is completely set with nets for a long distance up and down, and whether it is impossible for salmon to get up or down as it is alleged, it is evident from the results of the canning of salmon that the run of fish is very greatly impeded thereby. This is a very important industry, and while the government should avoid taking any steps that would be unjust to any of the parties interested, it would be well to preserve this industry for future years. The recklessness of American fishermen on the Columbia river has nearly destroyed a salmon industry on that river, which at one time was one of the finest salmon streams in the world. That has been the result of lavish fishing and the wanton destruction of the fish. The run of salmon is so reduced that I understand the industry is practically paralyzed. The same process is in operation on the Fraser river, beyond question. The "catch is largely reduced from year to year-

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
It cannot be otherwise ; anl the leaving of that river open for a few days for a free run of salmon in my judgment would be in the highest degree

advisable. I do not think that it is proper to jeopardize that industry in the interest of those wiho want for the time being to make a larger catch. X do not think any suffering will be entailed upon any one by following the course I suggest. It strikes me, from what X know of the matter, from investigation on the ground, that the mode of fishing in that river is certain to destroy the industry in a short time unless some course of this kind is taken.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
In reference to my bringing this telegram to the attention of the government, I do not think I was doing anything reprehensible at all. The telegram is from the secretary of the Canners' Association, which represents forty-five or fifty canners ; and they should understand, I think, what is in the interest of the industry as well as either myself or the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Morrison). They certainly are of opinion that the Fraser river is being depleted owing to the extensive manner in which it is fished, and that unless something is done, and done immediately, their industry will be destroyed. The fact is there-they are not putting up the fish this year. Although there is an apparent sign of a run of fish coming up the straits, it is a mixed run, which indicates that the good run of fish is gong-the run of sockeye, which is the fish they can for the English market, and which also brings the highest price in the Canadian market. I cannot see what injury it can do to any one to give them a close1 season such as they have always had until the last two or three years. The conditions formerly were different. The catches were coming up, and they thought there was no danger ; but now the catches are going down, and they realize that there is danger ; and, in order to avoid it, they ask for this concession. As the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has stated, it is in the interests of those who are more largely interested in that industry than any other people. They have an immense capital invested in it, and they surely would not suggest anything being done that would not be in the interest of that industry. I hope that the minister will yet see his way clear to agree to the suggestion made in this telegram. In regard to the truthfulness of what I have said, or any one else, the minister is able in an hour or two to get reliable information from his fishery commissioner on the ground, and I would be willing to abide by any representation he made on the subject, knowing him to be a man of good character, strictly honourable and honest, and knowing that he would not recommend anything that would not be in the interest of the industry, being on the spot and knowing the conditions that exist. If the minister has not already that information. I suggest that he immediately apply to that officer for information as to whether the statements made here are correct, and, if he
finds that they are, that he act upon the suggestion that has been made.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: The department has not neglected this matter at all. As sooon as the first telegram came, addressed to the deputy minister or to myself, I began inquiry about the matter. It stands to reason that the department is not going to decide on such a matter on the representations of one side only, and without inquiry from the proper officers in British Columbia as to whether the demands made are just and fair and reasonable. That is what I have done. As soon as the first telegram came, I began inquiring, and the information which I have, not only from the officials, is very contradictory indeed.' If the department had come to a conclusion without getting a complete report from our officers in British Columbia, that is to say, from the fishery agent there, Mr. Sword, we would have run the risk of doing a great deal of harm to the industry and the fishermen. The fishermen are the most numerous class of people, and their rights must be protected. If I am well informed, there is something extraordinary about this matter. I just give the information as I have received it indirectly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Have you a report from Mr. Sword ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Not yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: From whom did you receive this information ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I am not in a position to state. But the information which I have received is this, that the canners were under the impression at the beginning of the season that the run of salmon would not be very great. Under the circumstances they made contracts with the fishermen at a very high price, and the fishermen got very little, because the run was very small. But since the run has begun to be good, the fishermen are now getting a lot of money, and are making up for the time they have lost. The canners are not satisfied with that state of affairs, and if they could stop the fishing, they would break their-contracts with the fishermen. So there are two interests to be considered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Does that mean they would stop their own business in order to get lower prices from the fishermen ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: They would buy the fish on the other side from American fishermen, who use traps.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
On the other side they are in the same condition-they have not fish enough to keep the canners going.

The ' MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. That is not my information. My information is that the canners would get all their supply of fish on the other side from Americans, who are using traps, while traps are not allowed to be used in Canadian waters. Whatever may be the contentious on both sides, the department certainly would not do justice to itself if it were to come to a decision upon such an important matter as this without having a report from the proper officers in charge, who are responsible to the department for the carrying out of the law and the administration of the fishery regulations in British Columbia.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: In regard to the statement made by the minister that the canners are buying their fish on the American side, I may say that the American canners were coming over to the Fraser river and buying fish and putting up the price ; and the canners had come to an understanding with them to cease doing so. or they would go over and buy fish from the traps on the American side. So there is nothing in that. Referring to what 1^ said

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: I must call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that he has already spoken twice.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: With the permission of the House, I would like to say that ibis is a very important matter to the province of British Columbia. It is a matter wrhich I have pressed on the attention of the department year after year, in the time of the previous government as well as the present. I have pointed out that the trouble with the whole Department of Fisheries in British Columbia is that instead of being run departmentally, it is run politically.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: Not now.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may say what he likes. I had reports to that effect from the late representative of Bur-rard, who said to the late Minister of Fisheries that no man Should get the right to fish unless he got his consent. That was stated to the late minister by one of the largest canners in British Columbia, and a Liberal of the city of Vancouver. I have
no objection to mention his name

Mr. Bell Irving.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: When did he become a Liberal ?

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: He was always a Liberal. He may not have supported the school of Liberals to which my hon. friend belongs, but he is a Liberal of the old school, and always has been. Aside from that, if the Department of Marine and Fisheries is to to be run on these lines, the minister might as well throw it up and leave it to be run by the members representing the district. The way it is run now" is simply a farce.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext: No time should be lost by the hon. minister, but he should act at once in this matter. He can get official Information on which he can rely.

maintopic: SALMON INDUSTRY ON FRASER RIVER, B.C.
speechtext:
In view of the fact that I am pretty well interested in this matter myself, I would like to say a word or two in contradiction of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. When he makes the statement that the salmon business is run on the Fraser river by politicians, he makes a statement which I cannot qualify as being other than ridiculous. What the polities of Mr. Bell Irving are I do not know. The hon. gentleman says he is a strong Liberal, but he is reputed to have put up a good deal of money to defeat the Liberal candidate in the last general election, and a man who would do^ that cannot be a very sincere Liberal. I have had several telegrams in connection with this matter, which show that the canners are not at all unanimous. Here is one which I have received :
Canners not unanimous. If season closed will injure small canners and fishermen. Memorial not based on facts. Scheme to affect English market. Have written fully. Get Minister wait until properly posted.
He is one of the gentlemen referred to by Mr. McCraney.

I can assure my hon. friend that he who steals my purse steals trash, but he who filches me of my good name robs me of that which not enriches him and makes me poor indeed. It is easy enough to sling mud, but the hon. gentleman should be the last man to get up and throw mud at anybody else. People wrho live in glass houses should not throw stones. When the man is noti here to defend himself, the hon. gentleman ought, in common decency to reserve what he has to say against him for a future occasion, when he can say it to his face. The minister has acted perfectly right, and should not, under the circumstances, follow the advice of the hon. member for Victoria. It is well known that the people of Centre Victoria have been doing all they could to get the canning industry down there during the last five years. In the city of Vancouver, there are some hundreds of fishermen, not one of whom is in favour of having the season closed. The hon. minister should not do anything until he knows all the facts. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said that the nets were so closely placed in the Fraser river that they would not allow the fish to go up, but I know as a fact-and my statement can be proved by the papers-that the fishing industry in British Columbia has increased by leaps and bounds. This year is an off season, but I see by the Montreal ' Star ' that there are this year 170,000 cases packed in the river, and there are 300,000 in the

Columbia river. The Skeena river has been a failure, also the Naas, Rivers Inlet, and the Alaskan pack. If the canners get a good pack of sockeyes from now out, they will make money, because the pack is small in other places and will be next year as well, next year being an off year. It is always small every four years. When Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper was Minister of Marine, a howl was made to get him to extend the season, and the thing was done at the request <5f the canners. It satisfied everybody, the canners, the fishermen and the public generally. We found no request then to close down the season, but the reverse. I do not think it would be advisable for the minister to take the stand which the hon. member for Victoria has taken. I am prepared to stand or fall by the position I take. I do not think that this thing should be considered until the other side of the question is heard from-the fishermen as well as the small canneries.

The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Morrison) must have misunderstood what I said when he desired that the government should turn a deaf ear to any remarks I made on the subject. If he had paid attention to what I did say, he would have observed that I asked the government to give consideration to the subject. I do not know that there is any particular reason why the government should turn a deaf ear to a suggestion of that kind. If this is a matter which really involves the preservation of the fishery industry of British Columbia, the Minister of Marine should act promptly.
Surely not without information ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If my hon. friend had waited a moment he would have understood that I agree entirely in that suggestion. He should get all the information from his officers, and that as speedily as possible. But if he should dilly dally many days longer, and if there be any truth in these telegrams, the time to act will have expired. I entirely agree with the minister that if there is really an attempt to coerce the fishermen or small canners, the government should not listen to it for a moment. But he should carefully consider whether there is any foundation for that statement. It may be a difficult situation, but an administrative officer in his position has to deal with difficult situations and deal with them very quickly. I would suggest to him that there is the greatest possible need to urge expedition upon his officers in British Columbia, so that he may have the requisite information to deal with what is alleged to be a very serious situation. It is in the interests of the small canners and the fishermen themselves that this industry should be preserved.

What I meant to characterize as reprehensible is the giving of serious consideration to telegrams sent to individual members on either side of the House. We have an inspector of fisheries out there, Mr. Sword, a very reputable officer, who is right on the ground, and readily accessible to these people who are sending those telegrams. They could very easily consult Mr. Sword and have him communicate with the government. The hon. member for Victoria gets a telegram from somebody, I get a telegram from another and the hon. member for Vancouver gets a telegram from a third, and they are conflicting, and we come here and bother the minister, and there is not a word from Mr. Sword. Mr. Sword is keeping away from these squabbles. The very fact that the inspector of fisheries has not sent in'any communication, warrants the minister in not taking any notice of telegrams read from either side of the House. That is what I meant when I said that it was reprehensible for members on either side, in a matter of such importance, to ask that action should be taken on telegrams sent by interested parties.
Surely the hon. gentleman does not mean to say that, in view of the conflicting telegrams received by hon. gentlemen on both sides, the Minister of Marine should do nothing ?
He has done something.

He has not advised us yet what he has done. I rose for the purpose of asking the hon. gentleman what he has really done. I understand that the fishery commissioner is on the ground. Has the minister communicated with that gen- * Reman ?

I said I had. As soon as I got the first telegram I made' inquiry of Mr. Sword. I telegraphed him again yesterday to make a report to me by wire. I thought he might suppose that I wanted a report by mail, so I telegraphed him to send a report by wire.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
If the hon. minister had enlightened the House in the first place

*
He made that statement.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) made no such statement.
Of course I did.
I am not deaf, nor was I inattentive. I listened carefully to everything the hon. minister said ; and I am in the judgment of the House when I say the hon. minister made no such admission.

Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) will not say that the

lion, minister did not tell tlie House that lie had communicated with Mr. Sword by wire. I certainly understood him to say so.
I listened attentively to the discussion that has taken place, and, in my hearing, the minister did not advise us that he had wired to Mr. Sword and had asked Mr. Sword to wire his report.
I will have to say it in French next time, so that I may be understood.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I shall be glad to stand corrected if the hon. gentleman made that statement. I did not hear it, though I was paying close attention to every thing that was said.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir. Prefontaine) says he said it, and we here certainly so understood him.

I rose only to express my astonishment that, in the face of the information that had been furnished and of the urgency of the case, the propriety of calling the matter to the attention of the minister should be questioned by the hon. member for New Westminster (Sir. Slor-rison). I hope that, if the hon. minister receives a reply to his telegram he will lay it before the House.

I have just one word to say in connection with the contention, of the hon. member for New Westminster that it is improper for any individual to wire a member of parliament with regard to a grievance and ask it to * be brought to the attention of the House.
Under the circumstances.	.

I enter my protest against it. Every citizen lias a right to appeal to parliament for the redress of grievances in matter under the control of parliament, and he has the right to appeal to his own member or any member known to him ; and a member of parliament is doing the proper thing in bringing such a grievance to the attention of the government. That is their right, and their undoubted right.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask whether the government has any information to give with respect to the telegram which I read the day before yesterday on the adjournment of the House, with regard to the alleged action of the commissioners who were appointed to investigate the Trendgold concessions. I read the telegram, which I will repeat for the benefit of the right lion, gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) who is leading the House.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COSI-MERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). I would ask the hon. gentleman (Sir. Borden, Halifax) to bring this matter forward when the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is in his place. He will be here in a few minutes.

The Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), who was leading the House when I first called attention to the matter, said he would make inquiry and would give me any information the government might have at a later date, I bring the matter forward now to remind the government that the information was asked for.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AN DCOSI-M.ERCE. I will call the attention of the Prime Slinister to it as soon as he comes in.

House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the House to go into committee on a certain proposed resolution respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, and the motion of Mr. Puttee in amendment thereto.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT D. WILMOT (Sunbury and Queen's).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are confronted with one of the most important questions that have ever come before the Dominon parliament. Certainly, in my experience here, covering some fourteen sessions, nothing lias been brought before us comparable in importance with the great question we have now to consider. And, with my inability to deal with important subjects, I feel the very greatest embarrassment in attempting to address you to-day. I approach this question with feelings of awe at the enormous amount involved, the unknown millions that we are liable to be called upon to spend on this enterprise. I am also amazed, considering the small amount of information that is before us, that we are called upon to decide finally as to the merits of this question. Had we been experts in the professions of civil engineering, we might have given our opinion with some confidence. We are practically at sea. We have fragmentary information concerning one section of the country that this road is supposed to follow, and fragmentary information concerning another section. Yet, in the face of the insufficiency of information, we are called upon to say whether this country shall burden itself with liabilities for the great expenditure that will be necessary in order to carry out the proposed work. It is urged on the part of the government in forwarding this scheme that it is a matter of. I was going to say, urgency. I suppose that between urgency and emergency there is a distinction without any very great difference. I do not think, in

view of the past history of our friends who are in power, that they are exactly well fitted to deal with emergencies. It is well within rememberance of every one who hears me that a critical time in the affairs of our empire occurred, when the government was faced with a duty that devolved on them, a duty near to the heart of the whole empire, at all events to the heart of Canada- the duty of acting in defence of the empire. That was an emergency, and how did the government meet it ? The Prime Minister went off on an entertainment tour to attend some banquet, I understand in Chicago. But public opinion was so strong that the government felt that they were in an emergency, and, after some time had elapsed they repaired the mistake they had made. They acted, I may say, in response to the demand of the leader of the Conservative party. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, so far as we are concerned, I think there was something said about emergency rations during that campaign. They did not come out of that controversy with any great credit to themselves. Now we are face to face with a great emergency and from appearances I do not think they are going to come out of it with any great credit to themselves or to the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if a man goes to build a house he adopts the scriptural plan of sitting down and counting the cost before he begins. No such proceeding of that kind appears to have been undertaken by our friends on the other side of the House. \\ e know that is done by business men-and there are business men in the Liberal party, as good as any that can be found in Canada, shrewd business men who would not make any mistake in their private affairs, and how they can bring themselves to act as the government wish them to act on this occasion is more than 1 can comprehend. It must be an emergency. Where is the emergency 1 It is not apparent on the surface. We are told that that great country of which we are all proud, that great country north of Quebec and north of Ontario, is the country which the government are going to open up by their railroad policy as pro-jiounded by the right lion, the Premier. Well, Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to deny the facts of history. No one can charge the Conservative party wth having endeavoured by word or deed to prevent [ the developments of this great country, in the lives of every one of us, a great many duties will sometimes present themselves to us at the same time, and it is tlie part of wisdom to endeavour to perforin those which press upon us the most strongly at the time. Now, when we look at our great west, the extraordinary conditions that prevail there, the almost inexhaustible quantity of arable lands that are singularly fitted for producing all that man requires, lands that tlie world is beginning to recognize as the most fruitful for producing all the necessaries of life, is it not to our advantage, is it not our first duty, to turn our attention to them ? Let not our friends of the Liberal party take to themselves all the credit for these fortunate circumstances. They are only a small body of men controlling a comparatively small portion of the world, so far as population is concerned. Their influence is not so extended as that they have been able to bring prosperity to the neighbouring republic, they have'had no part in enriching the commerce of Europe. But all the same, Mr. Speaker,
I am willing to give those gentlemen the credit that they deserve.
Now, Sir, we must all acknowledge that that great country in our Noi;th-west would no more than be known at the present time were it not for the policy pursued in the past by the Conservative party. The history of the past points plainly to the fact that not only does the Conservative party deserve credit for having opened up that country, but it also points to the past that our friends of the Liberal party placed every impediment that they could devise in tire way of the Conservative party in carrying out their policy. The difficulties of nature were great, but not greater than the difficulties that were placed in their way by the Liberal party. Those difficulties brought the enterprise almost to the breaking point when the company called for further assistance, and at that time where did we find the Liberal party ? We

found them, as it were, step by step fighting against the advancement of this country, endeavouring to prevent the passage of that great measure which proved to be so beneficial to the Dominion of Canada. Who did we find allied with them at that time V We found the Grand Trunk Railway, a powerful factor aiding and abetting the Liberal party. When I say ' powerful factor,' I mean that they made representations in the money centres of the world, particularly in London, decrying the credit of the men who were working for the success of the enterprise that has proved to be of such vast benefit ,to this country. Happily, Sir, the combination of the Liberal party with the Grand Trunk Railway Company failed. When the difficulties appeared to be almost insurmountable, when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were also in extremes, and were obliged to come to this parliament and ask for a loan of $30,000,000, that proved to be almost the breaking point in the enterprise, but the men who governed the country at that time had faith in the future, and proved to be equal to the situation.
We all know as a matter of history that the money was advanced, credit was given to them at that time and that that great enterprise was carried to success. We all know the rest, and in spite of the influences then brought to bear that country was opened up and now I hope that the Liberal party do not take to themselves the whole credit for. the success that has attended it. The same Grand Trunk Railway Company, whose action at that time was most ungrateful. are very much in Evidence in this case. They were indebted to this country for aid in the construction of their own system to the extent of many millions of dollars, and they should have had a more kindly feeling for the welfare of Canada than to take the action they did at that time. Now they are again allied with the Liberal party, and I think that in view of past events we have strong grounds to look, if not with suspicion, with precaution, at the progress of events. I know that in the lower provinces, when it was rumoured that the Grand Trunk Railway Company were behind this scheme and were going to extend their railroad to the North-west that rumour was received with grave suspicion. It is well known that their eastern terminus is at Portland and that the distance to Portland. as compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway line to the port of St. John, is nearly 170 miles in favour of Portland. Our people in the maritime provinces also knew that the affiliations of the Grand Trunk Railway are very largely with the United States, and this knowledge created a feeling of further uneasiness when we learned later that they were the support of the strength and power of the government of this country. It then became a serious matter.
As I said before, I must protest against

the onus being cast upon the Conservative party of opposing the development of this country.
I wish for a few moments to attract attention to the proposed road so far as it concerns the province that I know better than any other, and which playi an important part in this scheme-the province of New Brunswick. Now, it is proposed by the scheme as outlined by the right lion. Prime Minister to carry the line through the centre of the province. We have, I will not say a great deal of information, but we have sufficient information, to understand what sort of a country that is. As an example, I shall read an extract from the report of Sir Sandford Fleming, submitted to the Canadian Legislature in 1865, in which the obstacles of the central route were concisely stated as follows :
In seeking to avoid the great military objection to any line in close proximity to the American boundary. Sir Sandford stated. ' we unfortunately increase the engineering difficulties; as. in looking for a line sufficiently distant from the frontier, Unless we at once go to the other side of the province, and thus considerably increasing the length, we are driven into a section of the country characterized by great irregularities of surface and difficult to penetrate.'
The difficult country from Rivi&re du Loup to Edmundston is described in the report. Next, the peculiarities of the Restigouclie river headwaters, not far from Edmundston, are noted.
As early as 1849 the country was reported upon by Major Robinson. His estimate was equally unfavourable. He wrote :
The fourth obstacle is the broad and extensive range of highlands which occupies nearly the whole space in the centre of New Brunswick, from the Miramichi river north to the Resti-gouche. Some of these mountains rise to an altitude exceeding 2,000 feet.
Further he states that:
The Tobique river runs through them, forming a deep valley or trough, which must be crossed by the direct line, and increases greatly the difficulty of passing by them. The lowest point of the ridge overlooking the Tobique river, at which any line of railway must pass, is 1,216 feet above the sea. Then follows a descent to the river of 796 feet in eighteen miles, and the summit level en the opposite ridge or crest between the Tobique and Restigouche waters 920 feet above the sea, or a rise of 500 feet above the point of crossing at the Tobique water.
The line down the St. John river valley does not present these formidable difficulties. In 1860. Mr. T. S. Rubidge reported on the route along the river above Woodstock. He wrote :
From Edmundston the line will continue down the valley of the St. John, at very favourable grades, passing through a comparatively well-settled, fertile and level part of the country. And long straight lines and curves of large radius may also be obtained here.

He further noted that:
The streams to be crossed are unimportant, but their valleys are sometimes very broad, necessitating heavy embankments

Although this article which I am about to read is the opinion of a Winnipeg paper, yet it is very appropriate to the country through which the line will pass in New Brunswick. One of the chief reasons, and, under the circumstances, one cf the most absurd that could possibly be given for the construction by the Dominion government of a line from Quebec to Moncton, paralleling the Intercolonial, is that it will effect a saving between the two cities of about one hundred miles, as compared with the Intercolonial route. In the first place there is nothing to show that any such saving will be effected. The Hon. Mr. Haggart, formerly Minister of Railways, has said that the saving will be only about fifty miles.
Granting, however, that the distance by rail between Quebec and Moncton is to be reduced one hundred miles by the building of this line, does this saving justify the condemnation to unproductiveness of the Intercolonial for all time, so far as interest on its cost, $68,000,000, is concerned. The interest at 3 per cent, on this sum is $2,040,000, to which must be added the rental of the Intercolonial's terminals at Montreal, amounting to $140,000 per year, making a total of $2,180,000, which the government is willing to pay annually to effect a saving of one hundred miles between Quebec and Moncton for the Grand Trunk Pacific. Surely such a saving does not warrant such an expenditure.
But there is another phase .to this question. If the saving of one hundred miles to the Grand Trunk Pacific is worth $2,180,000 annually to the government, then Halifax is completely out of the race with St. John as a freight port, for it is one hundred miles farther from Moncton to Halifax than from Moncton to St. John, and this difference cannot be in any way lessened. That being the case, what is the object of building across New Brunswick from Edmundston to Moncton in order to secure a point from which lines run both to St John and Halifax. Why not proceed direct from Edmundston to St. John, instead of running across the province from the extreme west to Moncton, which is almost in the extreme east, and then having to run back westward nearly ninety miles to reach St. John. _St. John is some miles nearer to Edmundston than is .Moncton, so that at least a hundred miles would be saved by building direct from Edmundston to St. John. If the saving of one hundred miles between Quebec and Moncton is worth $2,180,000 per year, surely a similar saying between Edmundston and St. John is worth an equal amount.
If to put St. John and Halifax on an equal footing for the securing of traffic, as will have to be done, the through rates to the two ports are the same although the haul to Halifax 313
is one hundred miles longer than to St. John ; why cannot the freight to these ports be hauled an additional hundred miles over the Intercolonial at the same price as will be charged over the shorter line that the government is talking of building. It will be as short by the old Intercolonial to St. John as by the now Grand Trunk Pacific to Halifax. If a one hundred mile haul makes no difference in the one instance? why should it in the Other ? The traffic which would thus be secured for the Intercolonial would put that line on its feet and enable it to pay interest on its cost, instead of being as it is now, operated at an annual loss.
The government will have to find a better excuse than the saving of one hundred miles in order to justify the building of the line from Quebec to Moncton for the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in advocating and endorsing the opinions that have been very clearly and convincingly expressed by members on this side of the House, X must repeat that I believe the proper way and the most direct way to get to the seaboard is down through the valley of the St. John river. The figures were quoted by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes), and I may be pardoned for giving them to the House again. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme from Levis to Edmundston via Connors is 166 miles, from Connors to Chipman 135 miles, and from Chipman to St. John 76 miles, making a total of 377 miles.
What is the distance between Chipman and Moncton ?

In the neighbourhood of 60 miles in a straight line, and it is an easy country through which to build a railway. Now, from Quebec, via the St. John valley the distances are as follows ; L6vis to Edmundston via Connors, 166 miles; Edmundston to Fredericton. ISO miles; Fredericton to St. John, 65 miles, making the total from L6vis to St. John via the St. John valley, 411 miles. I shall take the distances as mentioned by the right hon. gentleman, the Prime Minister. From Edmundston to Moncton, following an air line, it would be somewhere in the vicinity of 200 miles, but in going to St. John I recognize that we stop at Chipman, and from Edmundston to Chip-man it is 135 miles; from Chipman to St. John is 76 miles-that is, going from Edmundston to St. John partly by the government route and the Chipman route to the Intercolonial Railway, and it is 135 miles, making a total of 377 miles.
Now, while the distance down the valley of St. John is 411 miles as compared with 377 miles, we must recollect that the northern part of the road as proposed by the government runs through a country such as has been described by Sir Sandford Fleming, and which is a most difficult country for railway construction. If we take into consideration the grades that will be encountered, and the detours that will have to be taken by the government road, it will,



I believe, be a longer line of railway in the end than if it were built through the valley of the St. John. The route by the valley of the St. John is nature's route. It is through a level and fertile country, it is traversed by a railroad the entire distance, and its grades are all well known. The grades are not particularly heavy, although for a transcontinental road, no doubt, they could be improved at a very moderate cost.
I strongly advise the government, if they persist in this policy of extending the transcontinental railway from Quebec to Moncton, that they take that course.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in calling Moncton a terminus, it seems to me that we are asked to stultify ourselves. It is not a terminus. It is a point on the Intercolonial Railway overlooking a small tidal river, which is practically muddy ground when the tide is out. It is altogether insufficient for the purpose of shipping produce of any kind in large quantities that might come from the western country or elsewhere. It is, in fact, altogether out of the question as a point of shipment. As this paper says, why go off there ? It is a mere sentiment. To use a common expression, there is nothing in it-nothing of a practical nature. It does not help Halifax, while it injures St. John. Why go off there, for the sake of suiting the' political sentiments of the representatives of a certain portion of the province of Nova Scotia ? They must have a strong influence with the government when they can induce them to adopt that line. It is a mistake. If the object of this transcontinental railway is to pass from ocean to ocean by the shortest route, why take the long route ? Why divert the line for any purpose, except to avoid some natural difficulty ? Why not go to the seaport nearest at hand ? The proposal which I make to our Nova Seotia friends is this, to bring the line down by nature's route, the valley of the St. John, which is the most thickly settled portion of our province, to a common point at Fredericton, and from Fredericton branch off to Chipman and Moncton.

Twenty-three miles. The distance from Fredericton to Moncton could be shortened by having a short branch from the Canadian Pacific Railway to Fredericton. That would avoid the necessity of going down to Fredericton Junction, where the Fredericton branch meets the Canadian Pacific Railway. The adoption of this route would overcome the difference of opinion that exists, would do away with the proposed compromise, and would meet the requirements of the most direct and shortest line through the province of New Brunswick to the sea.
With regard to the central route, through the heart of New Brunswick, I am ready
and willing to acknowledge that while great natural difficulties present themselves to the carrying of the line through that section of country, such as the height of the mountains and the fact that the rivers have to be crossed at right angles, yet as a farming section it is one of the best in the province of New Brunswick. Aroostook county, in Maine, adjoining New Brunswick, is celebrated throughout the United States for its fertility. The large cities between Boston and the province line are to a great extent supplied by the products of that Aroostook country. I mention that to show that the same fine quality of land extends easterly, well across the province of New Brunswick to the Restigouche river. No man in that province knows better than does the hon. gentleman who has represented the county of Victoria in this House ever since confederation, the correctness of what I say as to the fertility of the soil of that country.
It is almost useless for me to advocate the claims of the valley of the St. John river ns the shortest route to the sea, because those claims are amply justified. But I consider it my duty to advocate them, because at present we are like people beating the air-we do not know whether the proposal of the government is going to be carried out or not. The air is thick with rumours that strong influences are being brought to bear upon the government, even within the last few hours, to abandon the whole project. Whether there is any truth in those rumours or not, I am not prepared to say. I will, however, quote from a journal which stands very close to those who support the government's proposal. The most doubtful feature of the government's transcontinental railway policy is the projected extension of the air line from Quebec to Moncton. is bold and progressive, and thoroughly meritorious in many of its features, and we are satisfied that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier would now so far revise his bargain with the Grand Trunk as to abandon the Moncton section, and declare for Intercolonial extension to the lakes, his action would be taken as an evidence of strength, rather than as a confession of weakness, and he would then present to the country a transportation policy which could not be successfully opposed.
In conjunction with that article, I was very much impressed with the speech delivered by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). That money, the ex-Minister pointed out, could be much more profitably spent in opening up and equipping our lakes, ports, and seaports and our water routes. Mr. Speaker, while realizing how precious is the time of the House at this late period of the session, I deem it my duty to explain-and I shall do so as briefly as possible-my position on this very important question which is submitted to our consideration. As the various aspects of the government's policy have already been dealt with in the numerous and able speeches previously delivered, I shall confine myself, in order to avoid repetition, to making some observations of a general character.
For eleven years past I have taken an active part in politics, I have followed closely public affairs, and it struck me that we were confronted with a great problem. For three years back. I have had the honour of attending the debates of this House,

and here also I noticed that this same problem, which is that of our means of transportation throughout the country, was being frequently discussed by the leading men and by the great papers of Canada, in connection with the enormous increase in our production, in our trade in general and in the needs of colonization. Everywhere, public opinion was awaiting impatiently the solution of this ever increasing difficulty.
Various plans were being discussed, the most important of which, to my mind, were the improvement of our inland water routes, the building of our canals, the proposed extension of the Intercolonial to the great lakes with a view to constructing a new transcontinental road, and the scheme for the building of a second Canadian Pacific Railway, all undertakings of a costly nature, requiring millions of dollars to be carried out. I followed closely the discussion which took place oil that subject, both by listening to the speeches and by reading ' Hansard,' as I was anxious to obtain a full grasp of the question. Speakers on both sides of the House have taken great pains, and I think I am in a position to decide knowingly, intelligently and consi'ceutiously on that great issue now before us.

What we want is to be able to put our wheat on the car and run it through to the seaboard. There has been too much money spent trying to create an artificial port-trying to make an ocean port out of something that was never intended to be so by nature. If half that money had been spent on the port of Quebec in providing proper facilities there-where we have a port that can float the largest ship that will be built in the next twenty years-and if we had a railway running from the centre of the territories right into the port of Quebec, from where our produce could be shipped twelve months in the year, you would not hear anything about the car shortage we hear so much about at present.
What we want is a continuous line of railway from the west to some ocean port, and Quebec is the proper place.
A prophecy which events are carrying out to-day. In the course of last year, the promoters of the Trans-Canada railway decided to form a company and laid before
the country the question of the expediency of building in the northern part of the Dominion a new road from Port Simpson, on the Pacific coast to Quebec, Ha Ha bay and Chicoutimi, in the east, as summer ports, and the maritime province ports as winter terminals, by means of the Intercolonial. Quebec and St. Catharine's bay, near Tadoussac were also contemplated as winter ports at some future date. Once the winter navigation of the St. Lawrence has been made practicable, which, I hope, will be pretty soon.
The road as projected, ran from one end to the other, through entirely new districts of the west, Ontario and Quebec districts abounding in wealth of various sorts. By means of branch line to Winnipeg, it gave the whole country the benefit of the shortest route, of the lowest gradients, and besides an all-Canadian route both as regards its location and its terminals. We were thus made entirely independent of our good neighbours to the south, who, under present conditions in Canada, profit immensely by the improvements we carry out, without ever showing us any gratitude.
Important meetings were held at Quebec attended .by the leading men of both parties for the purpose of considering the scheme, which was unanimously pronounced to be superior to all others heretofore laid before the public. It was decided to start a movement in Canada to spread the idea and have it accepted if possible.
Then it was that a further scheme for tlie building of another transcontinental railway was launched before the people. It was to be undertaken by the Grand Trunk Railway, to have its starting point in Ontario and to reach the west by way of Winnipeg. In the eastern part of the province the present system of the Grand Trunk was to be utilized.
I had the honour of being one of a delegation of the Trans-Canada sent to the maritime provinces to discuss both schemes with business men there. We met the boards of trade of St. John, Moncton, Truro and Halifax ; also members of this House and men .of high financial standing.
The discussion which took place was a business-like one; the feeling seemed to be general in favour of building at once, a new transcontinental railway, farther north, along an all-Canadian route both as regards its terminals and its location. Some boards of trade, particularly that of Halifax, passed very strong resolutions in that sense. At these meetings the expediency was discussed of building another line from Quebec to the maritime provinces, the Intercolonial being too long to enable the ports in those provinces to compete successfully against Portland. That idea appeared to be accepted generally.
About the same time, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) visited the west, meeting a great number of business men in

various cities ; and from- newspaper reports and other sources, the idea was gathered that there also public opinion was unanimous as to the necessity of a second transcontinental, provided it was all-Canadian.
Such was the state of public opinion at the opening of this session, and I arrived here firmly convinced of the immediate necessity of a new transcontinental further north. The Trans-Canada scheme was, to my mind and to that of many others, the most practical. While public opinion was thus concerning itself with this important question, and while some were favouring the construction of a Canadian transcontinental railway, and .others favouring the improvement of inland navigable routes and the building of new canals ; and others still favouring tiie extension of the Intercolonial, the government were discussing the same question in their secret councils. From time to time utterances of some prominent men would give us an inkling of what was going on. On certain days reference was made to the extension of the Intercolonial westward, while on other days, the question under discussion was that of a common trunk line for all the railways from Quebec to Winnipeg : hints thrown out to the public as to what the government were doing. The request for a charter on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the construction of a transcontinental was the first step towards feeling the pulse of the House. The Trans-Canada stepped in ; the struggle between the various interests was often a hot one ; but the north and east gained ground, and the original scheme was amended to meet their views. The plan of building a transcontinental railway through the northern country was accepted, and both the public and the House were awaiting anxiously the action of the government.
Finally, the government have come to a decision, and having satisfied themselves as to the necessity of a second railway throughout Canada, they requset the House to sanction the decision they have come to as a result of their investigation ; that is to say the building of a new all-Canadian route, as demanded by public opinion..part-of which to be built by the government and to be free of access to trade generally, and the remainder to be built by a company, with the idea of utilizing it both as a colonization road and a trade route.
