(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I would have been glad to get through with my remarks before the House took recess ; however, at the risk of wearying lion, members, I wish to lay before them a few more facts in connection with this matter.
In the first part of my address, I was endeavouring to show that the idea of building Mr. GIRARD.
another transcontinental through unsettled territories was not a new one ; that it had been discussed for some time past, and that if the government propounded such a scheme it was in response to the urgent demands of the people. The cabinet is charged with undue haste, for entering into this agreement without sufficient information on hand. But, if I am not mistaken, the location of the road is not yet settled, and the government will have to order surveys for which they will be wholly responsible. After considering the data supplied by these various surveys, they will be in a position to select the most suitable location as regards colonization and trade, which it is the object of this road to promote.
As for the section from Winnipeg to Quebec, the most direct line between the two points passes north of Lake Abitibi, whose waters empty into Hudson bay. By following exactly the height of land, the chances are that you would meet the poorest farming lands, and those that are the least favourable for lumbering operations, as in the vicinity of the sources of streams, these cannot be utilized either for the floating of the timber or the generating of power. Besides, the steepest grades would likely be found along that route, and the object it is proposed to attain would be lost. On the other hand, by locating the road further north, all these drawbacks are avoided.
As regards the section from Quebec to Moncton, the great objection is that the government is to parallel the Intercolonial. If my information is correct, there are at present two or three charters granted to private companies to do exactly the same thing, presumably with the assistance of the country. Moreover, as I stated a moment ago, at the time the Trans-Canada was being advocated in the maritime provinces, I got the endorsation and unanimous support of the business men down there in favour of the building of that line. I fail to see what difference it makes for the Intercolonial that it should be paralleled by a government-owned line, or by a company line subsidized by the country. The reduction of the mileage is the all-dominating principle in the matter. Besides, such a road will open up for settlement new districts, well adapted to agricultural pursuits, and which, otherwise, in Quebec, at least, will never be cleared.
It has been stated that the wiser course to follow would be to improve our inland waterways, as they afford the cheapest means of transportation. I followed the discussion on that point with the utmost interest. The arguments brought forward were based mainly on the experience of the United States, and to my mind, the results are not conclusive, but rather contradictory. Certain advocates of that idea laid before the House series of figures going to show that in some parts of the United States the bulk of the traffic goes by way of the water route and not by rail. Other hon. members

have given figures showing that in other parts of the United States with access to the water routes the bulk of the traffic is carried by rail. So that the contention set forth in the first place, although sound apparently, is only partially true as regards the movement of trade in the United States. In order to arrive at a true estimate of the comparative values of the water and all-rail routes, it will be well to observe what is going on in our own country. I refer hon. members to ' Hansard ' as evidence of the truth of my statements.
Advocates of the water route contend that railways cannot possibly compete with it. At the same time they tell us that the Canada Atlantic, a road which parallels the St. Lawrence river, and the bulk of whose traffic will, we are told, consist this year of
20.000,000 bushels of United States grain, is a paying concern, so much so that the suggestion is made that the government should acquire it and utilize it for extending the Intercolonial. Surely, these two propositions cannot be made to agree. If the Canada Atlantic is in a position to haul grain so profitably at the rate of two cents a bushel, despite the competition of the famous water route, the proposed route from Winnipeg to Quebec, taking into account their comparative mileage, could carry the same traffic at the rate of nine cents a bushel. Well then, what does the alleged superiority of the water route amount to ? Wherefore I say, let us consider what is going on in our own country ; we will learn more thereby than from any information gathered from the experience of the United States, which may be applicable to their conditions but not at all to ours.
Things have been so managed in the pasl that the hundreds of million dollars applied to the development of the country's trade have been expended for the especial benefit of southern Quebec, Ontario and the west. The city of Quebec, with its natural advantages, its ideal port, its three railways converging into it, has not received the attention which it should. She is waiting patiently that her children cease to consider her as a stranger, and that common sense be allowed to prevail.	.
Nobody complains ; the whole country rejoices ; the western country is growing by leaps and bounds ; everything is done that can be done towards its development. In this connection, one remark I heard seemed to me most regrettable. An hon. gentleman on the other side, discussing the scheme under discussion, exclaimed :	What is the
province of Ontario going to get out of this government scheme ? In answer to that question let me put another : What did the province of Quebec get out of our past policy ? I could hardly believe that a representative of Ontario would take such a narrow view of the question. For it should not be forgotten that the future of the whole country is now at stake, and local interests
should not be in the way of the general progress of the Dominion. As a result of the old policy, Ontario has been riddled with railways and improvements of all kinds, and the province of Quebec left, so to speak, to go barefooted. The people of Ontario should in the future show as much patriotism as the people of Quebec have shown heretofore. The prosperity of the country as a whole will ensure that of every province.
The results of the last census are now before us. Ontario and the maritime provinces will lose ten representatives, who will be replaced by ten new members from the west; and yet for only five or six years past have emigrants begun to pour into that country. Where has the missing population of the older provinces gone to ? The west has received a goodly number. However, Ontario praises its northern country, its - New Ontario ' as a paradise on earth. Quebec speaks in the same strain of the Lake St. John, Gaspe and north of Montreal regions. Are we not face to face with a most entrancing problem to solve ?* Should we not urgently adopt a broad policy which, while not interfering with the present system, will enable the older provinces to keep abreast with the increase of population in the west, and to retain in the administration of the public affairs of the country the position to which they are entitled. The government answers : Yes. I believe they are right. The piecemeal policy of colonizing followed in the provinces is not satisfactory. We have the proof before us ; it is necessary that the Dominion government should step in to give a new impetus to the settlement of the country ; a great artery of commerce is required at the right place, to supply all parts of the body with proper nourishment, in order that they may form a well balanced whole. That is apparently the aim of the government scheme.
Information is sought, doubts are raised, as to the character of the land in our northern country. At all events, it is contended that they cannot compete with the lands of the west. The inference would be, I presume, that we shall have to wait until the west is filled up before we think of colonizing the northern parts of Ontario and of Quebec. To my mind, Sir, if I may be permitted to say so, that principle is false and almost unpatriotic.
What information is required to convince people in good faith that our lands in the north, are good, equal to those in the west ? Have not accounts of them been given for two hundred years past by missionaries who roamed over this whole area ? Have not official reports been published by direction of the governments of Ontario and Quebec? Is it assumed that explorers like the Bells, the Sullivans, the Dumais, the Bignells, and others, like McKenzie, of Montreal (who has just returned after discovering there rich deposits of asbestos) is it assumed that all those men have written jokingly, without

leaving their desk, works of imagination as it were ? Have we not the oral testimony of our trappers and hunters, and even of Indians, handed down from generation to generation and preserved in our homes ? All that is' sufficient information to me ; it is good evidence of the fertility of the soil, of the wealth of the forests, of the suitability of the climate, not to speak of the mineral resources of the country, of the fisheries of Hudson bay, which our neighbours to the south seem to appreciate better than we do.
Now, when the scheme for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway was brought forward, was there laid on the Table of the House information as complete as what is required to-day from the government ? So that, to my mind, these data are sufficient to satisfy the government that the construction of a railway through that region is quite feasible, and practicable. I extend to all skeptically inclined an invitation to visit the country I have the honour to represent. We are there, due north of Quebec, on the brink of the great northwestern table-land, with the Lauren tian range to the south and east of us, and the limits of the province to the north and west. You will find there lands that give wealth and happiness to the settler within a period of a few years. You will find that the crop returns for that district are greatly in advance of those for the rest of the province, equalling at times those for the west, and last year surpassing them. You will find there a small farming community-grouped around the towns of Chicoutimi and Rober-val, two new stars of the north-whose numbers have increased fifty iter cent within the last decade, a result observed in no other part of the province. That is due to the construction of the short line of railway built from Quebec to Lake St. John and which has been fully operated since 1893 only. But at the time, despite the natural advantages of the country, and on account of the distance, the want of means of communication, the people were losing heart. In some localities the parish census has not even shown the average increment. In 1901, eight years later, the Dominion census shows, in that same district, the increase I have just stated. That small community of settlers exported last year six million pounds of cheese, five hundred thousand pounds of meat, two hundred thousand bushels of grain, besides what quantity of those products was consumed on the spot. If a short line of railway from Quebec to Lake St. John has, in the space of eight years, accomplished so much, what may we not expect from a great government railway opening up all at once this whole region ? We are only a few people down there yet; we have only a few acres under cultivation; and there are still 70,000,000 acres of that land, covered *with virgin forest, drained by large rivers, Whose roaring water-falls of incalculable Mr. GIRARD.
power await impatiently to be turned to advantage by the hand of man. As regards education, the seminary of Chicoutimi, the convents, the school of domestic economy, of Roberval-the only one of its kind in the country-and	the numerous parochial
schools will show that in no respect are we lagging behind the times.
To return to the great water powers, let us see what is going on on the rivers of Chicoutimi, JonquiSres, Ouiatehouan and Peribonlca. The four pulp mills built on those streams have a capacity of 520,000 tons of manufactured pulp, present output : and the quantity of barked pulp wood shipped out is just as large, making a total of 1,040,000 tons.
The lumber trade is just as large, though the population is only 30,000, and there only four small rivers operated. What enormous business will be developed when the rivers Ashuapmachouan, Peribonka, Mistassini and others will be put to use with the great forests they drain. Not only will these products of the forests be available for export, they may be shipped to supply the needs of the western country, and by themselves would provide enough freight to sustain the railway. Official data confirming what I have just stated concerning this district were received on the day before yesterday at the Department of the Interior.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, let me say one word in reference to some unfavourable comments made on our lands as compared with those of the west. My contention is that our lands are just as valuable, provided they are not beforehand despoiled of their natural wealth. Of course, if in this district which is to be opened up, the present provincial laws were to be enforced, the settler would go west, and rightly so, as he would have a better chance there. But let the Dominion government and the governments of Ontario and Quebec have a conference before taking any action ; and let them study together the best means of putting to advantage this projected railway, and all will come out right.
If, in accordance with the present practice, the timber and the water powers are turned over to outsiders, who despoil the land of all the settler needs to make a living for himself at the outset; if, moreover, the mineral resources are also reserved, then we may expect the same failure there as the returns for the last decade show to have been the lot of the older provinces. But if pains are taken to find out the adapti-bility of the various districts to farming or to lumbering operations, if agricultural belts and forest belts are located along the line, and if the farming lands are sold to the settlers in their natural state, with all the riches they may bear or contain, then our lands will be as valuable ns those in the west. The settler will take them up with the assurance that he will not at the outset suffer from want, for lie will have at his

door the raw material of a great industry which he can put on the market at any time to supply his needs.
Put up the selling price of these lands, if you wish, retain the fees, that will not interfere in any way ; you will not have lost anything, and you will see the settlers come in great numbers as in the west, eaeli township having its period of lumbering at the outset, while farther on, in the parts not suited or not reserved to farming, the lumbermen will carry on their business on a larger scale, but all together working hand in hand for the general welfare of the community. You will see no more of those disputes between the settler and the lumberer, disputes of which we hear so much and which are so harmful ; and the danger of forest fires bi'eaking out will be minimized, as the settler will be just as interested as the merchant in protecting the forest, as well as his buildings, both equally precious to him.
But under present conditions, the settler, especially in those parts where the pulp industry has been carried on, having on his farm only stumps and wood of no value, is anxious to get rid of them as soon as practicable, and his best means of doing so is fire.
Now, if, in the west, the government before selling them to the settler, leased the lands to companies or individuals who robbed them of their original wealth and left them to the settler minus seventy-five per cent of their value, do you think that the tide of immigration towards the west would be as strong ? Why not deal with our wooded lands in the same manner as we deal with our prairie lands ? The time is no longer when the settler meekly believed his lot was to suffer. We shall have to look to him, Mr. Speaker, in our northern country, to render us absolutely independent, commercially speaking, from the neighbouring states. Sir, I lay that suggestion before those in authority ; it is worthy, I believe, of their serious consideration.
Now, on going over the data supplied for the Trans-Canada, as did my hon. friends the members for GaspS and Bellecliasse, and others, I am led to believe that it is in that direction that the grades are the easiest for heavy traffic. The greatest difference of level between Roberval and the western boundary of Quebec is 1,200 feet, spread over a perfectly smooth table land, where there is not a single mountain in sight, not even towards lake Abitibi,-and that according to surveys made especially to ascertain differences of level. With that in view, the promoters of the Trans-Canada had offered to carry all the grain from the west, whatever the loading point (even along the Winnipeg branch) to the port of Quebec or to Ha Ha bay, at the rate of nine cents per bushel. They could afford to do that, as their route would be a direct one, without transhipment, without the use of elevators and the delays they involve. Besides, the
offer was made to carry the settlers free of charge. Under those conditions, there was to be a net profit of $1,416 per train of 30 cars, or 52 per cent. Is it necessary that a railway should bring such large profits to be a paying concern. I do not think so. And those figures were obtained by a capable engineer, Mr. Doucet, and verified by men of weight, such as Messrs. Wm. Price, J. G. Scott, Tanguay and others.
The bon. Minister of the Interior has given as possible a rate of 11 cents per bushel along the road which they propose to follow across the country. These two estimates are of a nature to convince us that, in the absence of a transcontinental water route, inland navigation is not and will not be in a position to compete with the all-rail ropte, especially when we take into account the reduction in mileage and greater speed secured by following the latter route. Now, since the government have the same object in view as the promoters of the Trans-Canada, and will run their railway through the same country, will they not be in a position to offer as low a rate ? Let them follow the same route, and that will settle it.

In spite of all that has been said, I fail to conceive how the longest and slowest route can be the easiest and cheapest. I stick to the belief that the most direct route is the shortest and the cheapest. Moreover, I am of opinion, that nations, as well as individuals, should, under all circumstances, unless radically prevented from doing so, control their affairs the year round, independently of their neighbours. I think I have shown by statistics that the future of the country is dependent on the northern country ; in that country lies our hope.
In that way, Sir, do I appreciate in a general way the scheme which the government has just laid before this House. I would have preferred the Trans-Canada. I did all my power to gain my point with the government; they deemed it their duty, in the interest of the country at large, to propose something else. I must give them full credit for acting in good faith ; I am satisfied that they were moved under the circumstances by very serious reasons. If it was necessary that twenty years should elapse before the Canadian Pacific Railway be paralleled, at the rate things are going, within ten years from now, the Trans-Cana'da will have to be built.
My district may have benefited in a greater measure from the Trans-Canada scheme than from the one under discussion; but the government are aware of what is going on there. They know that within two years, the stream of settlers which is pouring into that district, and which they have helped to such an extent for the last seven years, will come to a standstill if railway is not extended from Roberval westward. Already we have settlers 70 miles away from the railways. The government are aware that an important company is awaiting a decision in the matter to begin utilizing the enormous water power of St. Feli-cien. They know that it is necessary the railway should be pushed on from Chicoutimi to St. Alphonse to open up for general trade the magnificent seaport of Ha Ha bay to which I have referred. They are satisfied that the river Saguenay should be deepened as far up as Chicoutimi, or even Shipshan, in order to promote the great, industries of Chicoutimi and those in course of creation at the point I have just named, and at the Grande Decharge. The government know that it is proper to provide a winter steamboat service on the Saguenay, from St. Catharine's to Tadousac. They are aware that the extension of the Roberval road to James bay, in connection with the present line, would almost be equivalent to the Trans-Canada. of our district that he has gone thither to lay the foundation of a great carbide, iron and pulp industry ; with Mr. B. A. The inference is that he approves of the government having done so, and that he would have acted similarly under the circumstances.
The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) referring to the Trans-Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the 26th of May last, said :
It is a road from Quebec, I gather-for we get pamphlets about it every day-and it is to run through to Manitoba and the Northwest. I do not know who the promoters are or anything about it. But, if the Grand Trunk Railway propose to build a road into that section of the country that is another matter. The Grand Trunk Railway has done a great deal towards the development of this country, and the stockholders of that concern have had but meagre return on the money they have invested. Anything the Canadian people can do in return for the great benefits that that company has yielded to this country ought to be done, other things being equal. If they propose to build a road which -will open up a new territory in the North-west, and make a connecting line with Quebec, I would rather see it assisted than any other scheme I hear proposed. (3446 of Debates.)
As I said before, we have a choice of deciding between two companies for the building of this road. My opinion is that if the government should decide to give any assistance for that purpose, the company which is entitled to the preference is the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That company has done a great deal to open up this country, they have spent a great deal of money, and have received very littlte return for it. (3448 of Debates.)
Should that hon. member, au ex-Minister of Railways, were in power to-day, would he think otherwise ? In the Senate, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, leader of the Conservative party seconded the motion to grant the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific. All that goes to show that that company has powerful supporters on all sides.
I am satisfied that the time has come for northern Quebec to have its equitable share. I am convinced that the northern country

Is the comer stone of our country's commercial independence, and that the plan of the government is the most practical means of maintaining the present political balance In the country and increasing our prospects of trade in the future. I consider that the scheme laid before us is a good one, and on the whole is deserving of the country's approval. One of the promoters of the Trans-Canada, a Conservative of Quebec, wrote to me, last week : * From the national standpoint, there is no doubt in my mind that the policy of the government for the building of a road from Quebec to Winnipeg is a good one and will greatly benefit the province as well as the whole of Canada.'

6. Scott, the leading promoter of the Trans-Canada, in the ' Morning Chronicle,' of Quebec, expresses the same views. Mr. Doucet, engineer of the Trans-Canada, stated to me a few days ago that the government scheme, as regards Quebec, was on the same lines as that of the Trans-Canada, according to which the railway was to run direct to Quebec from the north of Take Winnipeg, with one branch line to Winnipeg city, and another from James bay to Ha Ha bay and St. Catharines. So, I am not alone of that opinion : the engineer of the Trans-Canada scheme believes that the government scheme is an equivalent one as regards Quebec.
It has been stated that the projected line, will not have any traflic and that its usefulness will be nil. I have heard it said,,, especially this year, as a cardinal principle, that trade, like water, has its natural channels. If that be so, in accordance with the figures I have quoted, the western and the general traffic, once the projected line is built from Winnipeg to Quebec, will naturally take its course that way. So that apart from the local trade which will be considerable, traffic will not be wanting, provided the line is rightly located.
Some express fear at the heavy expenditure entailed by this undertaking : $100,000,000 and more, it is alleged. The government put down the expenliture at $13,000,000. There must be a mistake somewhere ; the discrepancy cannot be so great. I understand the government to mean, that the only amount expended that will not bring in a return, is the interest during the first few years, as the road will remain ultimately the property of Canada, the company, in the meantime, paying interest on the capital invested. In fact, our public debt will be increased by those $13,000,000 or so, and no more.
Now, in projecting to build the Trans-Canada, we were prepared to expend $100,000,000, and that, to build a road through an entirely desert country, where everything had to be provided. What would these same people have thought of such an undertaking when they fret at the thought of engaging into the building of

a road which can expect for its first train as much traffic as it can haul ?
What would be the cost of the alternative scheme proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition ? The same amount. He stated that the people of Canada are not afraid to spend their money for useful improvements. What would it cost to improve our waterways, as proposed ? Millions and millions of dollars.
So, we are confronted with various proposals, all of which entail, let us say, to avoid quarelling, all the same expenditure. I think the proposal of the government is the best because it benefits all the provinces in a more equitable way than does the proposal of the leader of the opposition, which would strengthen still more the present system of providing for the requirements of one part only of the country, and besides would leave us at the mercy of the United States.
Praise has been bestowed on the system of local or branch colonization railways. Sir, we have had enough of that system to know what it is worth. It took twenty-five years to build 170 miles of railway from Quebec to Lake St. John ; and for eleven years past, the company has not found the means of building the remaining ten miles to connect Chicoutimi with Ha Ha bay, in accordance with its charter and its most solemn pledges to the government and the public. They cannot be prevailed upon to extend their road west of Roberval, although warranted by the requirements of the settlers and the prospective establishments of large industries at St. Felicien.
And see the Gaspe peninsula which has remained stationary, notwithstanding its natural advantages, awaiting those vaunted colonization roads. See the country to the north of Montreal, the Nominingue, the St. Maurice valley. Why not admit it at once, that system is too slow, surrounded by two many difficulties.
Times have changed ; we have no more that old-time settler who believed himself destined by Providence to a life of privation and suffering, his sole reward to be the honour of having founded a new colony. The struggle for life Has changed : the poor as well as the rich strive now only for comfort. Hence that unfortunate desertion of the country, that aversion of the settler for our forest lands, in recent times, and that wild rush towards the western prairies to the detriment of the older provinces. Since, therefore, it is necessary to build railways in advance to ensure the success of colonization, and since the provinces heretofore have been unable to do better with their railways than follow at a distance in the footsteps of the backwoods settler. I consider it our duty to accept and to further the proposal that is made of providing a great central railway through the finest forest territory remaining to us. I speak from experience. I have partaken of the settler's life in the backwoods ; I know.'

its difficulties. I know what are the views in this respect of the community I represent ; and I think I am the faithful interpreter of every settler in the province of Quebec when I say they rejoice in finding a government providing for them through the forest a royal road which will do away with the misery of old.
Not very many years ago, a man who is no longer with us. laid on the Table of this House the Bill for the first transcontinental road through Canada. What a surprise. What dark forebodings. What conflict of opinions. Millions to be spent, in-suffiicent data, and what not. None. Sir, are better acquainted with that phase of our history than those of my colleagues who were then members of this House. Sir John A Macdonald and his supporters persisted ; the Bill was passed as being a good measure on the whole, nothwithstand-ing imperfections of detail. Twenty years have since gone by. That scheme has been found so beneficial, that even his political opponents are prone to say that Sir John A. Macdonald was a great statesman ; and following in his footsteps, request to be authorized to build a second transcontinental. The new scheme is criticised in the same way as the former ; but the parts are interverted.
History repeats itself and I trust it will do so in this case. Some day Laurier will disappear. Ontario will pride itself in having given birth to Sir John Macdonald and in having his remains ; Quebec will pride itself as to-day in having given birth to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the country will honour the graves of these two eminent men each with its brazen crown ; the one bearing the letters, C.P.R., the other G.T.It. Around these two graves two great races who have founded Canada will feel themselves more tightly bound one to the other by a common sentiment of national pride.
Sir, I realize that the vote I am about to give will be the most important act of my political life. I represent here enormous interests ; I was elected by an intelligent community to whom I honestly promised to support the government whenever possible. I am favourable to the principle involved in the measure, and I believe it to be superior to all' others which have been discussed in this House, as it decentralizes the commerce of the country, and is more equitable to all its parts. At the same time, the rejection of the Trans-Canada scheme, whereby my best and most devoted personal friends felt greatly aggrieved, might have induced me to oppose this Bill. But. after closely following the debate I am satisfied that the Conservative party would have dealt with the Trans-Canada in the same mood as the cabinet. Besides. I recognize the substantial assistance which this government has given to my county on all occasions, as well as the cqurteous treatment I received at the hands of its members. I am confident that the Prime Minister is taking an ever increasing
interest in the welfare of my district, and I would, for all those reasons, deem myself greatly failing in faithfulness and in honour, should I in such a solemn circumstance of his life, refuse to uphold his views. In so | doing. I believe I am fulfilling my duty conscientiously towards my country, my province, the constituency I represent, and towards my friends, and I entertain the hope that all will be benefited in a large measure by this policy.

I regret very much. Mr. Speaker, that I am not sufficiently well versed in the French language to have understood the arguments of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Girard) who has just taken his seat, which I have uo doubt have been very able and interesting. It may be quite true that nearly all the arguments that can be advanced, either for or against this scheme now propounded by the government, have been brought forward ; at the same time there are people iu every constituency who have a right to know where their representative stands on an important measure of this kind, and therefore it is that I shall address the House on this occasion. I realize that hon. members on both sides are becoming impatient at the prolonged nature of this debate, and I can assure them that it is my purpose to make my remarks brief. I am strongly in favour of the development by railway of those parts of this Canada of ours that have not yet been opened up, but I desire to see measures for such development undertaken by the government only after serious inquiry, and on the basis of the .very best information that can possibly be obtained, and in a manner which shall be found in the best interests of the country. I am willing that money should be freely spent by the administration of the day on any railway that will have the effect of improving our transportation facilities, in opening up unsettled districts, and generally in drawing the provinces of this confederation more closely together. But I believe that this scheme propounded by the present administration, coming as it does without that information that we on this side of the House consider necessary to have been obtained by the government, has been conceived in reckless haste, and is not one that should appeal to the country. Since this debate commenced, arguments have been brought forward on this side of the House which ought to lead the government serious ly to reflect before deciding to embark in an expenditure of such an immense sum of money without the necessary information which would justify them in doing so. I believe that the Grand Trunk Pacific should be afforded every facility for getting into the North-west, and should be granted liberal assistance for that purpose, under reasonable and safe conditions.
I consider the proposal that has been ' brought forward by the government to be

defective in many ways. I desire to call attention to a few arguments that have no doubt been previously given in this House, but which I think can bear a little repetition. In the first place, I would call the attention of the government to this fact, tliat now for the first time in the history of the country a great railway corporation is to be bound to the government, and the government is to be bound to that corporation for the period of fifty years. Fifty years, Mr. Speaker, is a long time, and the results may be very serious to the country. I desire to call attention to some points in clauses 7 and :l(i of the contract entered into by the government with the Grand Trunk Pacific. In clause 7 it is provided :
In order to insure for the protection of the company as lessees of the eastern division of the said railway, the economical construction thereof in such a manner that it can he operated to the best advantage, &c.
As I desire to shorten my remarks as much as possible, I will only read the portion of the clause I wish to refer to. Clause 16 provides that the government are bound to consult tlie Grand Trunk Pacific as to the amount of money that shall be put into the eastern division, and that it shall be economically constructed. Then clause 16 provides for betterments. Now it is well known in railway construction in this and other countries that the first construction is not usually intended to be a durable one. I contend therefore that the clause leaves it open to the Grand Trunk Pacific to secure the construction of that eastern division in such a way, in so economical a manner, that every year thereafter betterments will be called for and the government will have to provide them. - Now, this is clearly shown by these two sections, that in each year a large sum will probably have to be spent for betterments, and I have no doubt, in my own mind, that the amount that must be spent in this way will come to even more that the interest that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will have to pay on the cost of this road.
A good deal has been said about the security that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are giving to the government for the payment of the 3 per cent interest upon the cost of construction of the eastern division. I was rather amused not very long ago by hearing a gentleman who came from a western Ontario constituency, represented by an hon. gentleman on the government side of the House, state that the government had a perfect ' cinch,' as he elegantly expressed it, in the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company; that they were secured for the payment of all they would expend in building that portion of the line by a mortgage on ail the rolling stock on the whole line. I asked him if he was quite sure about that, as it was not the manner in which I had read the contract. He said : Oh, yes, the member for Mr. WARD.
my county told me so. I should think that hon. members should be careful about wbat they say to their constituents in reference to this contract, and should really stick to the truth when they undertake to instruct them upon this very important question.
I shall deal very briefly with the cost of construction of the eastern division. So many different estimates of this have been made, that really any hon. member could be excused if he had not a very lucid or clear idea as to what that division is really going to cost; but there can be no doubt in my mind that it must cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $75,000,000 to $100,-
000.	If that is so, as the security given is only a second mortgage upon the $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock which are ear-marked, I believe, for that division, what security can there possibly be after the rolling stock on that division has commenced to depreciate ? The hon member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) brought forward what I thought was one of the most conclusive arguments as to the danger this country is incurring in constructing that eastern division. The argument which he brought so clearly before the House has not been answered by any hon. gentleman opposite who has followed Kim. He argued that as the earnings of the Grand Trunk Railway itself, on its roads in the thickly settled portions of this country, only amounted, after paying working expenses, to $800 per mile, that in this sparsely portion of the country through which the eastern division of the Gi'and Trunk Pacific will run, they would have to earn even a larger amount per mile in order to pay the interest on the cost of construction, even taking this as the amount which the government admit it will cost. It seems to me that this contract which has been entered into by the government was stamped as unbusinesslike at the very outset; if we are to believe what we have heard in connection with the negotiations with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway people, they absolutely and entirely refuse to undertake the construction of that portion of the work. That being so, it seems to me that the project is stamped at once as being an unbusinesslike one for the government to enter into.
The right hon. gentleman who brought down this scheme, and he did so in very eloquent language, used that expression which I suppose lias now become historic; ' We cannot wait.' It seems to me, with all due respect to the right hon. gentleman, that the reasons he gave to the House and to the country for the undue haste with which this project is being carried out were not of a very serious character-in fact, I might almost say that they were flimsy. The right hon. Prime Minister, in excusing the haste with which this contract was entered into, expressed great fear that the bonding privileges would be taken away from us; and in connection with this excuse,

I will read a short extract from the Minneapolis * Journal.' It is as follows :
The Grand Trunk Pacific scheme has caused a strange twist in the attitude of the Canadian parties toward the United States. The Liberals have generally been supposed to be the party of those who had no ill-will for or special fear of the republic, but Sir Wilfrid Laurier is advocating a Grand Trunk Pacific on the ground that there must be an all-Canadian route which cannot be affected by the withdrawal of the American bonding privilege. The Conservatives are now answering that there is no danger that the United States will ever withdraw that privilege. And they are right. Uncle Sam is riot prone to cut off his.nose to spite his face, and with the growing sentiment in the United States In favour of freer trade with Canada, there will be no tendency to get rid of such encouragement to trade as we now have.
This is an expression of opinion from the Minneapolis ' Journal,' and it seems to me that from what we know of the American people, that there is not the slightest danger of this bonding privilege being withdrawn. It is not at all likely that the American people, and the American government, entered into this arrangement with Canada years and years ago, unless they were going to reap from it at least as much advantage as the Canadians would. It has been a general feature of our dealings with the Americans that they generally get a little the best of the bargain; that they derive the greater advantage, and I am quite sure that we have nothing to apprehend in the danger of this bonding privilege being removed.
Several lion, gentlemen have spoken of the congestion of freight that has taken place ill the North-west in the last two years. That congestion, I believe, has existed with the two last crops grown in the North-west, but such arrangements have since been made by the railways already in existence in the west as to enable them to cope with the difficulties in a much better
manner than in the past. Now, I wish to call attention to the estimate of the crop yield for the last two or three years: Year.	Estimated Yield.
1898	 31,450,000
1899		 34,830,000
1900		 17,055,000
1901		 63,300,000
1902		 67,000,000
1903	(highest estimate) .. ..	58,000,000
Thus, the estimated crop for this year is nearly 10,000,000 less than that of last year. Of course, that is a matter to be regretted, but it shows that there is not the necessity for haste, so far as the moving the crops in the North-west is concerned, is the right lion, gentleman would lead us to suppose. The project might, in my opinion, very well have waited for another year, and the country would not have suffered in consequence. The commission which has just been appointed by the right hon. gentleman's government was, as I supposed, a commission to take into consideration the very points
which have led the government to introduce this scheme to the House.
Now as the government have decided upon this great transportation scheme, that commission seems only of use to register the decree of the government already issued. We always imagined that the commission was appointed for the purpose of trying to solve the transportation problem, and it seems unfortunate that the government should have rushed this matter before parliament with unseemly haste before the commission had an opportunity to tender its advice upon it. Let me read an extract or two from a speech of the Prime Minister delivered some years ago, to show what a change of heart has come over him. On the 21st December, 1880, Mr. Laurier, as he was then, had this to say with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway contract then before parliament:
The policy of the Liberals was that it should be built gradually as the wants of the country require and its resources permit.
The policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to-day is not to build his railway gradually and as the resources of the country require, but to rush into it without knowing what he is doing. Again the Mr. Laurier of that date said :
Honourable gentlemen opposite will remember that they received ample warning not to create that state of things which -should bind this country to the immediate completion of the road. They were reminded that if they did so they would be putting a burden on this country too heavy for its strength to bear ; but they did not heed these warnings, they forced their followers to vote for this policy, and how, as a crowning consequence of that policy, their followers are asked to consent to enormous sacrifices involved in this contract. . . . In my humble judgment it was a crime, though I might say without severity it was a political crime-at all events it was a fault to bind this country to the immediate construction of the road.
I read that to show that the right hon. gentleman at that time believed in making haste slowly, and did not believe in rushing wildly to construct a railway as he is doing in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.
The Liberal party in Canada seem to have realized lately that the Conservative government made no mistake when they built the Canadian Pacific Railway, and, as they built it. The hon. the Finance Minister! told us the other night that he did not refer1 to the Canadian Pacific Railway contract with the intention of casting any reproach whatever upon the men who framed it and Who constructed that railway. That was a considerable admission for the Finance Minister, a leader of the Liberals, to make, and I commend him for it. We of the Liberal-Conservative party have always contended that the proper system to adopt was to build the Canadian Pacific Railway as a harmonious whole, and not a thing of shreds and

patches, as the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie proposed ; and, Sir, subsequent events have abundantly shown that the Conservative government was right. The policy of Mr. Mackenzie was to build the road In four sections, and after giving the contractors $10,000 a mile and 20,000 acres per mile, to hand each section over to them to be thereafter owned by these contractors. That would have given us four different sections of railway running between Lake Nipissing and British Columbia, while the Conservative administration by sticking to the original scheme, have given to Canada a national highway of which every Canadian is proud.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce when speaking to this motion, told us that the remarks of the Finance Minister met with his entire approval, and so he did not devote much of his time to the consideration of the question, but applied himself t* one of his old time speeches in condemnation of the railway and fiscal policies of the Conservative party. I am glad the right hou. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has come into the House at this opportune moment. Here are his words :
However good the record of the Canadian Pacific Railway may be looked at as a commercial undertaking and I think the future historian of Canada would largely bear me out when I say that no possible combination of blunders could be conceived or could be more injurious to Canada than those which marked the initiation of that enterprise. I say in the first place that the bargain which they made in 1871 with the people of British Columbia by which, without knowing the smallest circumstances or the smallest fact that they ought to have known, they bound themselves within ten years by a treaty with that state, unasked for by them, to construct that railway was a fatal mistake, a mistake which resulted in very great injury and very great loss to the people of Canada and which serioftsly affected the permanent usefulness of the road.
But the right hon. gentleman did not tell us in what way the interests of the country had suffered, nor did he in any manner show how the permanent usefulness of the Canadian Pacific Railway has been impaired by the policy followed by the Conservative administration. I desire to call the attention of the House to his word, ' unasked for by them," which I would take to mean that the province of British Columbia did not ask for the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The right hon. gentleman must have forgotten the history of the time, or, he would not have made such a statement. I quote from - the memoirs of Sir John A. Macdonald, by Joseph Pope, an extract which X take to be correct:
In June, the death of Governor Seymour gave to the imperial government an opportunity of showing their appreciation of Sir John Macdonald's judgment. Mr. Musgrave was immediately transferred from Newfoundland to British Columbia. Through his influence, aided by the efforts of the Hon. (now Sir) Joseph Trutch, and other friends of the UI>-on, an

agreement was entered into, the principal condition of it being the construction by Canada of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In the autumn of 1870. the people of British Columbia approved this arrangement, at a general election. On the 20th of the following January it was ratified by the legislature, and on the 20th of July the waters of the Pacific ocean marked the western limit of the Dominion.
The government of the _ Dominion undertake to secure the commencement simultaneously within two years from the date of the union, of the construction of a railway from the Pacific towards Rocky mountains, and from such point as may be ^elected, east of the Rocky mountains, towards the Pacific, to connect the seaboard of British Columbia with the railway system of Canada ; and, further, to secure the completion of such railway within ten years - from the date of the union.
That, I apprehend, conclusively answers the hon. gentleman when he says that the Canadian Pacific Railway wras not asked for by British Columbia.
Does my hon. friend want to know the facts ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext: I only know the fact that the hon. gentleman has stated! what Is not correct.
The hon. gentleman is very much misinformed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
In addition to that, I wish to show that the Liberal party of that time were distinctly against the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, more especially the British Columbia section. On the 16th of April, 1S80, the Hon. Edward Blake moved the following amendment to a motion of Sir Charles Tupper in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway :
To leave out all the words after ' that ' in the said motion, and to insert the following instead thereof : ' The public interests require that the work of constructing the Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia should be postponed.'
The Hon. Edward Blake, in concluding his very able speech on that occasion, made use of these words :
Complete the railway to Red river, go on with the prairie section as far as settlement demands. For that risk something, since the die is cast. But in order to succeed in that, in order that you may have a chance later to do more, deal with that alone now. Bend to that great effort your undivided energies, your whole available resources. Postpone meanwhile the western work, and do not by your present action, based on airy dreams and vain imaginings, risk the ruin of your country.
That was the position of the Liberal party at that time. Their policy was simply to build the railway as the necessities of the country required It; to drop off settlers, I supposed at the western end of the road, and only build into the prairies towards British Columbia as in their opinion the

necessities of tlie country required. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if that policy had been carried out the Canadian Pacific Railway would not have been completed to this day. It seems to me that with the lack of energy which characterized the administration at that time, they would have simply gone on building small portions of the railway, and Canada would not have been in the position she is in to-day, to enable these hon. gentlemen to pose as the administrators par excellence of this country. That is one of the colossal blunders which my hon. friend referred to as having characterized the policy of the Conservative administration of that day. The completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The hon. gentleman also referred to the arrangement which the government of that day entered into with British Columbia as a colossal blunder. I leave it to the good sense of the House to say whether or not the hon. gentleman's charge is correct. He went on to state that he had an interview or correspondence with Sir Stafford Northcote, the chancellor of the exchequer. This is what the hon. gentleman said :
I very well recollect that when I came to lay my proposition before Sir Stafford Northcote, while he admitted the substantial truth of my suggestion that the road was of imperial concern, that its construction would be a great benefit to the whole British empire ; he told me nevertheless in so many words ; that although he believed that my request would have been acc3ded to at once at the time that the union of British Columbia was affected, yet, that as we had chosen to bind ourselves by treaty to the people of British Columbia to build that road within a certain period of time, it was out of his power under the circumstances to propose to the British parliament to grant us any further assistance.
The hon. gentleman evidently bad no confidence in the resources of the country at the time the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie's administration was in power. He was afraid to launch out into the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway without assistance, and therefore he made this frantic appeal to the British government to help him over the difficulties which he seemed unable to overcome himself. It seems to me that that was rather a humiliating position for the hon. gentleman to take, after the courageous policy that had been enunciated and partly carried out by the Conservative administration.
The hon. gentleman also had his usual fling at the Conservative administration for the small number of immigrants that came to the country during the eighteen years that Sir John Macdonald's government was in power. That argument of the hon. gentleman's is so old that it hardly needs any answer. But I would, call his attention to this fact, that while the government of which he was the Finance Minister was in power, the exodus to the United States went on just the same. It is a matter of con-314
gratulation to all the people of this country, onl both sides of politics, that we are now getting large numbers of immigrants from the United States, instead of our youug men leaving our shores and going to that country. But surely the hon. gentleman can not claim that as a result of the present government being in power. Surely he understands, or he ought to understand, that the United States, being a very much older country than Canada, has been attracting immigrants for many years ; and that the stream of immigration, having once set in, in any particular direction, it is a most difficult thing, I imagine, to stem the tide, and divert it in other directions. That has been, in my opinion what we have had to contend with. Every immigrant who went to the United States was an immigration agent for that country, and used his influence to bring his friends there. I am very glad to say that the tide is turning in our direction, and I am sure that no one rejoices over that more than the Conservative party.
The Hon. Mr. Tarte, in the speech which he delivered to the House the other day, remarked that he regarded the debate which has been in progress for the last three weeks, as a peculiar one, in this respect. He said :
One thing is cheering ; we have not heard anybody during this long and interesting debate talking blue ruin or talking about the absence of the credit of this country. On both sides hon. members of the House have expressed the fullest confidence in the future of Canada and in its ability to grapple with the biggest problems.
That is in strong contrast with the conduct of the present government when in opposition. As everybody knows, who has studied the proceedings of parliament at that time, especially when the Canadian Pacific Railway was being built and the National Policy was being introduced, a great many blue ruin speeches were delivered by these hon. gentlemen. But no similar accusation can be established against this side. No hon. gentleman on the government benches can prove that the present opposition have ever adopted any such course as was followed in the days I referred to by hon. gentlemen opposite. Judging by the criticisms, Mr. Speaker, indulged in by the supporters of the measure before the House, it would seem that they either do not understand, or wilfully misunderstand the policy enunciated by the hon. the leader of the opposition. In my opinion that policy is a broad and courageous one. It is, I believe, becoming every day more popular with the people, and I should not be surprised if the government, before this resolution is voted, were to adopt some of the suggestions made by my hon. leader. Were they to do so, they would be acting in the interests of the country. The policy enunciated by the leader of the opposition offers an attractive alternative to the vicious



policy enunciated by the government. In every line it suggests that we should not blindly rush into any scheme without counting the cost, and if the leader of the opposition should be returned to power at the next general elections-which we are told are very close-it would not even then be too late to modify this contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, so as to make it more acceptable in the interests of the country. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway themselves, I believe, are not altogether in love with the scheme, so far as the eastern division is concerned, and would be quite willing to modify it; and if that were done, it would save millions of money to the country.
Hon. members on this side have been charged by hon. gentlemen opposite with unpatriotic conduct, because they are opposing the measure before the House, but no accusation of preaching blue ruin has been or could be possibly made against us. The Conservative party rejoice in the fact that, in spite of the infliction of having its affairs conducted by a Liberal government, the country is prosperous. The hon. leader of the opposition, referring to the speech of the Minister of the Interior, tried to make out that there was no competition between railways and quoted as proof the high rate between Kansas City and Chicago. Now, I want to show you, from the report of the Interstate Commerce Commission, wherein the hon. leader of the opposition was mistaken. The annual report of the Interstate Commerce Commission for 1901 says :
During the past summer the open tariff from Kansas city to Chicago has been 12 cents per 100 pounds, bjit the actual rate at which wheat was moved has been as low as five cents.
That goes to show that while the rate was fixed and published at 12 cents per 100 pounds, and that rate was quoted, the actual rate paid by the people shipping wheat was 5 cents per 100 pounds, which was brought about by competition.
Now, I want to deal with something that the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has been hammering at in and out of season, as well as hon. gentlemen opposite, with reference to canals. They say that canals regulate the traffic. I want to read from the report of the Interstate Commerce Commission for 1900, which goes to show that the Erie canal between Buffalo and New York does not regulate the traffic, but that it is competition between railways that does so. That report says :
It has generally been understood that the canal frpm Buffalo to New York city, while it carried a comparatively small amount of the grain traffic, determined the rate at which the railroads should carry the balance, but Mr. Harriott testified that this was not true ; that the canal was not now a factor, either in the carrying of the traffic, or the making of the rate : that if the railway lines advanced their rates, the canal promptly followed ; that the controlling factor was competition between these railroad lines, and that if this competition could be eliminated, advances in rate would only be limited by market conditions at home and abroad.
There is the statement made by the Interstate Commerce Commission, composed of gentlemen who ought to know, that the Erie canal at the present time is not a factor in regulating rates, but that the railroads are. , Mr. Speaker, in attempting to address thell on se on the theme which has been the subject of debate for three weeks past, I do not suppose I shall be able to add either argument or information to what has been already said in the many speeches which have been delivered on both sides. Neither shall I attempt to follow the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) in the rambling and discursive address he has given the House. In speaking to-day, he has dwelt upon liis favourite theme, one that, I suppose affords him some satisfaction in addressing his constituents in the North-west. Abuse of the Canadian Pacific Railway seems a favourite form of discourse on the part of the hon. gentleman. I suppose it gives him the same satisfaction that that form of oratorical exercise so often practiced in the United States and known aa ' twisting the lion's tail ' gives to some politicians over there. And I suppose they are both intended to have the same effect in the elections. Whatever I might have to offer on this occasion, if there be no other merit in my address it will at least have the merit of brevity. Even if I had information and argument of great value to bring to the House, I feel that I have not on this occasion, sufficient command of my voice to address the House at any length.
I had the privilege and pleasure of listening to the very able, interesting and elo-

quent address made by the right lion, the Premier, in laying this scheme before the House. For, Mr. Speaker, I ana ready to admit that however I may differ from the right lion, gentleman in some of his opinions, however I may differ from him in the reasons which he gave for his policy, I am not insensible to the charms of oratory, and I will concede that his speech had at any rate the charm of oratory. It had all the polish of diction, all the beauty of rhetoric which could be brought to bear upon a subject of that kind, and the right hon. gentleman certainly acquitted himself in a very pleasing manner so far as the form of his address was concerned. He dwelt for two hours in the realms of romance. But we are not able to endure long flights of oratory, we cannot soar at such great heights for any length of time, we have to come down at last to terra firma; and when we get down to solid facts and examine closely into the proposition laid before us, we find that after all the speech of the right hon. gentleman was of a decidedly romantic and imaginative character, When he was about finishing that speech and came to his peroration, after drawing a vivid picture of all the glory of the great North-west, of the bright fields of waving grain, of the immense population that would flow into that country as a consequence of the construction of this railway, and when he said : Gentlemen, all this you can have for the small sum of $13,000.000-well, it did appear to be cheap, I acknowledge that it did appear to be what you might call a bargain. We have heard addresses of that kind before. It recalled to my mind the experience of my boyhood when I saw flaming posters announcing the coming of some great circus. When the day came and I beheld all the outward splendour of the decorations, and heard the orator outside the tent telling us of all the wonders that had been gathered together from the four corners of the globe, and after I had parted with all the pennies that I had saved up, to go inside and see these wonders, I remember how great was my disappointment when I found that the reality was almost a blank. There was about as much relation between the outside show and the inside reality as there was between the grand and beautiful picture which the right hon. gentleman presented to us as his scheme, and the reality that we found when we came to examine it in detail.
The right hon. gentleman told us that there was a feeling throughout this country, that it was universal in every Canadian heart, that the time had come when Canada must have another transcontinental railway. Now that was a big thing. I do not know, however, that I have been sensible to that feeling. I do not know that the people generally whom I meet throughout the country have been conscious of any such want. I know there is a feeling throughout the country which has been expressed time and again, which I think is a universal sentiment, that the time for bon-using great corporations in this country has gone by, that the time for giving away great land grants or money grants for the construction of railways, is pretty well past in this country. There might have been ai time, I think there was a time, when necessity did exist for assisting railway enterprises that were designed to open up new territory. There may be even at the present day occasions and circumstances that would justify parliament in granting such assistance, but no reason has been given to show that the present occasion is one of that kind.
Now, certain reasons were given by the right hon. the Premier why this scheme should be presented to the people. It was a surprise, I believe, to a great many members of this House. When we met here in the month of March there was no intimation that a transcontinental railway from ocean to ocean was in contemplation. We did know that there was talk of the Grand Trunk Company wanting to get access to the grain fields of the great west, and we were not surprised at it. It would indeed have been surprising if that company had not desired to enter into competition with other railway companies which were exploiting the great North-west. We were not surprised at that, and we were quite ready to believe that they would ask for some assistance, because we know that railways without exception are always ready to ask, and to take anything they can get out of the government, whether in land or money. But many members on botlf sides Of the House thought that if the Grand Trunk Railway wished to get access to the grain fields of the North-west there was sufficient inducement for them to build a railway into that country with their own capital, with their own means, without seeking any substantial aid from the government.
Now. when we make a comparison between this enterprise, as a means of opening up that country, and the old Canadian Pacific Railway enterprise, we find that the conditions are altogether different. We remember that even after that company was formed, even after the country had to some extent been opened up, capital was still very cbarry about taking any risks in it. We remember that the stock of the company was sold at as low a figure as twenty-five cents on the dollar ; and that it was a long time before it rose to anything like the ordinary market price of railway stocks, showing that it was regarded as a risky enterprise. Therefore it was an enteprise which required and deserved the support of the government, and I think this country has no reason to regret having given that support. Occasionally we find men like the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), who, perhaps, owes all the material prosperity that he enjoys to the privl-


leges that have been provided for him toy tlie Canadian Pacific Railway, who will still condemn the government of that day for having made liberal grants of land and money to that railway corporation. But I believe that there is, deep down in the hearts of all the people of this country, a conviction that the government did what was necessary under the circumstances, and that the consequences have fully justified its action.	i ,
Well. Sir. there is another very widespread feeling in this country, and that is against subsidizing railways. There are other cries also that are coining up to parliament from the people of this country. One of them comes from the manufacturers, who are asking for more protection* from the workingmen in the shops, in the factories, in the mine, in the fields, asking from this paternal government protection of some character. The government have turned a deaf ear to these requests, but when approached by a great moneyed interest like the Grand Trunk, they are quite ready to listen to it. Now we know that when any great project is launched in this country the first question asked is : Is there any money in it ? Well, I say there is money in this enterprise : there are millions in it. But for whom ? Not for the farmers of this country, not for the miners of this country, not for the fishermen of this country ; but there are millions for the exploiters, for the grafters, for the speculators. These are the men who are coming to this government to see what they can get out of it.
Now, let me ask where did this idea originate ? What was the genesis of the idea of another transcontinental railway ? Not with the masses of the people of this country, not with the farmers of Manitoba or the Northwest Territories. They do not call for another transcontinental railway from ocean to ocean. It is true, we are told there was a congestion, and I believe there was in some parts of the country, and the people were asking for relief. But it has been pointed out over and over again that the congestion was caused, not so much by want of new railways, as by want of sufficient rolling stock, by want of better equipment on the lines that are already in existence in that section of the country. I believe that there is a very faint idea in Canada of the extent to which railway building is being carried on at present throughout our north-western country. There is now a great mileage of railway under construction ; a great mileage already in operation is newly constructed with the ballast scarcely settled on it, and now we are projecting another great railway enterprise that will come into competition with them all. The congestion of which so much has been said, has already been provided for to a very great extent, although perhaps not entirely, because there were causes for it over which Mr. RICHARDSON.
the railway) companies, the Canadian Pacific Railway and others, had no control. They had difficulty, for instance, in getting all the rolling stock which they required ; industrial centres are sometimes hampered in their operation, and there was a difficulty in obtaining the rolling stock which they had ordered, and for which they were ready to pay. But, I understand, and believe, that this year there will be a very great improvement in that regard.
I say that the demand for the building of this railway did not originate with the farming class of the country ; it did not originate with the mercantile class ; it originated first with the Grand Trunk Railway -but their proposal was not for a scheme of this kind. It was undertaken by the government after coming into contact with some large moneyed men who thought: Here is an opportunity to add to our millions. The suggestion no doubt was given to the government in that way, and has been taken by them. It is a very taking suggestion, and came at an opportune time, for if. was necessary perhaps to divert the attention of the country from some other matters that should press upon it. I do not say that this session has been barren of legislation ; some very important measures have been put through. But still the government were ready to seize hold of this for all it promised them, for all there was in it to them. It is not a commercial enterprise ; it has far more of a political character than any great enterprise ever before projected in this country.
