When the House took recess at six o'clock, I was speaking of the reasons adduced by the government to excuse their great haste in pushing through this measure. The Prime Minister told us that a great crisis was upon the country, and that we could not wait, but he kept the House in the dark as to the nature and origin of that crisis. It certainly is not to be found in the alleged congestion of traffic in Manitoba or the Northwest Territories. It certainly is not to be found in anything which a man of ordinary information can discover, and therefore we have a right to ask : Why this mad haste on the part of the government ; why this haste in absolute disregard of the statement put in the mouth of the Governor General at the opening of the session, that a transportation commission would be appointed to get light on the subject ? We have been told in an off-hand way that there are mountains of information bearing on this government scheme, but nevertheless nothing tangible has been laid before parliament. Another excuse given for building this road

in such a hurry was that the bonding privilege might be abrogated, but that has been so exploded that no government supporter now attempts to resurrect such a bugaboo. It could only have been stated to the House by the Prime Minister in the hope that a lame reason and a poor pretense was better than no reason at all. Then, again, we had it stated from the treasury benches that if the scheme were not gone on with now, the Grand Trunk Railway might not be open at a future date to accept such a deal as the government is giving them at the present time. Well. Sir. it is not at all [DOT]credible that the Grand Trunk Railway would at any date be simple enough to refuse the benefits which they are getting under this scheme. They are not going out -of business in Canada ; they are likely to stay in the country, and they will be just as ready for a good deal with the government next year or the year after as they are to-day. As to this government road relieving the congestion of freight traffic in the west, that is an absurd proposition, because a scheme that will take at least seven years to carry into operation is not going to relieve the congestion of traffic in the near future. It is said also that it is necessary to have this railroad to open up new areas for settlement. Well, Sir, it must be evident to all that it is the greatest folly to open up larger territories for settlement than we already have, seeing that millions of acres already opened up are crying out or settlers. We have railways sufficient o accommodate 10,000,000 more people, if those railways were properly equipped and properly supplied with all the accessories that are needed to the successful operation of modern railways. When you have settlements at great distances apart you have to encounter great disadvantages, socially, municipally and educationally. Man does not live by bread alone ; he needs a larger life than the merely animal ; he needs social intercourse and all that it implies in culture, refinement and development. Isolation tends to barbarism, and one of the greatest difficulties we have to overcome in the settlement of our great North-west is that people coming from the larger social life of the closely settled districts of Europe become disheartened in a sparsely settled country. We need regular settlement to build up the country methodically, wisely and regularly. We need it for the culture, refinement and development of our settlers ; all of which are brought about by education, by religion, and by all those things that elevate the mind. We need regular settlement to furnish traffic to roads already built, to establish communities and to attract the best class of settlers to that country. It is a bad policy to build railways into new areas of territory that will not and cannot be settled for many, many years to come. It would be far better that we should have regular, consecutive settlement in our country. Again, I hold that it is not necessary
to have another transcontinental railway as a means of communication with our great North-west. Nature has given to us lakes and rivers which afford an easy and a cheap means of transportation, and nothing that is known to science, nothing that is known to civilization up to the present day, can equal our noble waterways as a means of transportation. The facilities for transportation by these natural water routes are developing wonderfully. It seems but yesterday since the traffic was carried in comparatively small boats, but now these modem whale-backs take such immense quantities of grain that no system of railway yet devised can compete with them in cheapness of transportation. We are not opposed, as a party, to any necessary expenditure for the development of Canada, if it be carried out on proper and in methodical lines. The history of the Conservative party in the past in regard to transportation, and to commerce, and to manufacturing, is a record of the development and the extension of this country. The Canadian Pacific Railway is a monument to the transportation policy of the Conservative party. To-day we hear Liberals' aclaiowledge that they were mistaken when they decried the Canadian Pacific Railway in days gone by, and that they are now willing to cheerfully admit that this great enterprise has brought honour on its promoters and upon the country. It would appear as if the Reform party, looking hack on the history of the past and regretting their want of foresight, were now anxious to make a history for themselves ; were anxious to build themselves a monument to show that they have lived and worked for something. And so, Sir, they conceived this mistaken idea that another transcontinental railway was necessary. We on this side of the House are opposed to all hasty, ill-considered measures. AVe believe that the sentiment of government ownership is growing in this country, and so far as railway construction is concerned, this scheme of the government will retard the realization of that idea for at least fifty years. The experience in government ownership of railways and telegraphs and telephones in other countries seems to point in favour of government ownership in this country. We cannot attempt, and it would not be wise for us to attempt, to bring it about at once in Canada, but we should aim at it. We have the beginning of government ownership in the Intercolonial Railway, and it would be a wise policy for us to experiment on it further, and to see if we cannot make the Intercolonial Railway a success in a larger measure, and thus fully test the principle. The best value that the' people of Canada get for their money comes to them through the postal service, and although it may have its faults as administered, it is the very best and the very cheapest service that is given to the people of this country, and it is managed by government. Not only in various coun-

tries in Europe, but in India, we have an object lesson of what government ownership is doing. Railways which have probably been built in that country for military purposes are now operated successfully and so as to pay reasonably well ; and all over India there is a railway service, with fair accommodation, at the rate of half a cent a mile for passenger traffic, though, of course, there is a higher rate for some of the higher classes of people. The government of India holds the telegraph service, the telephone service and the postal service, all operated satisfactorily and all very cheap.
Now, I swill touch for a short time upon the supposed cost of the government's project, and the absurd statement about $13,000,000 being the total amount which this enterprise will cost this country. In what sense do we own what we have not paid anything for ? $13,000,000 would appear to be the amount that is to be thrown away, absolutely wasted, in the initiation of this scheme-something for which there will not be any asset in the way of service or property ; nothing to show for It at any time from the beginning to the end. I know that the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross) asserted that he believed that that is all it would cost. He believed it, he said, because the Premier had said so.
What about the Finance Minister ?

I fear that there may be other people who may be willing to take it on the ipse dixit of the ministers. It was a mischievous statement, I think, and one which will bear a little looking into. The hon. member for South Oxford (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) used an Illustration to explain it. He said that if in buying a farm he mortgaged it for all he had to pay for it, it was not costing him anything ; he had borrowed the money which he was going to pay for it. But If be got no service from it, or was renting It for nothing for fifty years, I think he would feel that he was making a very bad bargain. I would put a question to the hon. member : Suppose he said to his son : John, I have an opportunity of buying a farm for $5,000, and I can borrow the money to pay for it at 3 per cent, so that all the farm, will cost us will be the interest that v e will have to pay on that money ; that is everything the farm will cost us. The proposition seems very fine to begin with ; but it is a different thing when he adds : John, I am renting that farm for ten years for nothing, and you must work hard to earn the money to pay the interest on it, and perhaps in fifty years It may come into our possession when we pay the full price for it. It is evident, I think, to the most shallow thinker in this country that to construct that road from Winnipeg to Moncton we shall have to pay the cost Mr. RICHARDSON.
of the construction, whether we pay it out of the supposed surplus or borrow the money to do so. We have to pay for it, or we do not own it. But the first cost of $13,000,000 is that which is absolutely lost-for which there is no pretense that there is anything had in the shape of service or pos-sesssion.
But this is only like some of the other hollow pretensions made for this contract The Prime Minister, when speaking of another part of the contract, said : ' There is something in this which I think will commend itself to the hon. member for Stormont and Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) ' ; and he read this provision :
The company shall purchase all material and supplies required for the construction of the western division and the equipment of the whole of the said line of railway from Canadian producers, when the same are produced in Canada. and when such material and supplies can be purchased in the desired quantities and of equal quality suitable for the purpose required, and for prices and upon terms equally advantageous with those procurable elsewhere.
Is not that something magnanimous 1 It is equivalent to saying to the producers of Canada : In connection with this great and costly enterprise you shall have the privilege of tendering and competing with the producers of other countries for the furnishing of supplies. And yet this is held up as a great preference given to the manufacturers and producers of Canada in connection with this great public work. I say these are hollow pretensions, unworthy of a great government. The cost is enormous, a tax upon the efforts of the workers of this country, which will be felt for a lifetime. We paid cheerfully for the costs incidental to confederation. The farmers of this country were quite willing, in order that the great North-west should be developed and the terms of confederation carried out, to create a great competition witli their own products, and to pay for that competition in the form of taxes. There has not been much grumbliug about that. There has been a magnificent national spirit displayed. But there is no necessity for imposing such burdens upon them to-day. Will there be no let-up to this enormous taxation for the opening up of new territories ? The confederation has been satisfactorily completed ; the terms of confederation have been grandly and loyally carried out. By no parity of reasoning is there the same claim on the taxpayers of this country for this enterprise that there was for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It may be said, what matters to us what the result will be fifty years hence ? We will not be called on to pay more than the first ten years' interest; let future generations look after themselves. I think the framers of the Ashburton treaty on the British side may have felt an indifference something like this. They may have said : It is possible that this patch of Maine run-

ning up into Canada, and which ought to belong to Canada, may make a difference to the country in the future ; but it will make no difference in our lifetime. Men who are nation builders do not act like this. This is not the method of the great men who build for the future welfare of their country. The pioneers of the older provinces built for the future ; they bore burdens and hardships such as we have not to experience. Men in the west, with overflowing plenty to-day, not knowing anything of the struggles of the pioneers of other days, or realizing what they owe to them, are impatient of results. We do not begrudge them having all the facilities possible. I believe the counter proposition made by the bon. leader of the opposition is one that will work far better for the well-being, prosperity and immediate relief ot the settlers in the great North-west than the proposition of the government. It works in harmony with the natural resources of the country and with our great lake and river transportation system ; it points to the extension of the principle of government ownership ; it means the saving of fully $50,000,000 to this country. This is a wise and statesmanlike proposition, whereas the proposition of the government is one which bears the imprint of haste, rashness and extravagance, and which suggests the warning contained in the old Latin proverb : Whom the gods would destroy, they first make mad.

I do not expect, Mr. Speaker, that I shall be able to say much that is new in connection with this very much. discussed subject, but I shall endeavour to express, as briefly as I can, my views upon it. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson), who has just taken his seat, was exceedingly complimentary to the leader of the government. In his opening remarks he admitted that he had listened with considerable interest and a certain amount of pleasure to the charming oratory of the right hon. gentleman. He admitted that he himself was almost convinced by the right hon. gentleman's persuasive eloquence of the propriety and wisdom of this policy ; and I wish to pay my hon. friend from South Grey this compliment, that I think he is the only one on that side who has spoken in complimentary terms of the leader of this government, or of any hon. gentleman on this side who has addressed the House on the subject before us. But let me here say that it is not by the charm of oratory alone, for which the right hon. gentleman is noted, that he, as leader of this government, has won his way to the hearts and sympathies and affections of the people of Canada ; it is not alone by his sunny ways that he has won their esteem, but by his sterling integrity of character, and the fact that he has given this country the best ad-315
ministration it has ever had. And let me add, that whenever he goes before the people, be that time near at hand or distant, the people will express their confidence in himself and his administration, and in the proposition which he has submitted to this House.
The hon. member for South Grey told us that although delegations had come here asking for protection for various interests, although representatives of the labouring classes had come asking for more protection, this government had turned a deaf ear to their appeals. Representatives of the farm, ing and other interests, he said, had come to the government seeking for the protection they desired, but the government had paid no heed to their complaints. But when politicians had come down with a large scheme on hand, for which they wanted government assistance, the government were quite willing to accede to their demands. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that the best and the only protection that can be given the labouring classes is to give them a market where there is a good demand for their labour at remunerative prices ; aud that is what this government is giving them to-day to a greater extent than ever before under any previous administration. And to our farmers, who are raising crops, not alone for the home market, but for foreign markets as well, who are producing a great deal more than the people of Canada can possibly consume, the best protection which the government can give is to provide them with abundant means of transportation by which they can send their products to the markets of the world with the least possible delay, and at the least possible cost. I would remind the House further that it is not true that our farmers and labourers have been calling on the government for protection in connection with their interests. I have no desire to take up the time of the House at any length in discussing the trade question, because it is not directly relevant to the matter before the House, but I wish merely to refer to it incidentally, in order to meet points which have been raised by my hen. friend and others in that connection. And in reply to my hon. friend, I wish to point out that not only did our farmers aud labourers not send delegations to this government asking for protection to their interests, but, on the contrary, they sent delegations protesting against any increased protection being given in certain directions, and insisting that the government should look after the interests of the farming and labouring classes as well as those of the manufacturers by not generally raising our taxation any higher.
My hon. friend said that there were millions in this project. Well, one can hardly expect a transcontinental railway to be constructed from end to end of this Dominion without there being millions in it. But evidently what prompted this remark was



the idea in his mind, conveying the insinuation that there were millions in this scheme for somebody who would not give any return to the country. That suspicion has prevailed to a certain extent in the remarks of a number of the speakers on the other side, but has no foundation in fact. Where did this idea of a transcontinental rail-way originate, the hon. gentleman went on to ask. There was no demand, he said, for a transcontinental line. Let me inform the hon. gentleman, for his benefit, that, as fains the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) is concerned, the idea of a transcontinental railway originated in his mind when in Vancouver. It had already been spoken about, but at Vancouver the ex-Minister of Railways expressed his thorough approval of the policy of building such a line, and of doing so with the shortest possible delay. The hon. gentleman went on to argue that the congestion in the west has been provided for, that there is now no special urgency for the construction of this road, that there was a time when there was urgency and special need for this road, but that that time had gone, and there is no longer any pressing necessity for its construction. Well, assuming that the position he takes is a good one, it is in direct condemnation of the proposal of his own leader, who desires that we should accept the scheme he has put before the House.
I shall not endeavour to touch on all the different points which have been raised in connection with this subject, but shall merely take up two or three as they present themselves to my mind. My hon. friend then alluded to what he termed the bugaboo of the bonding privilege. Evidently hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the cue from their leader, to ridicule the argument advanced in connection with this privilege by the government. But any one who is at all familiar with the history of this country knows well that the Americans have on several occasions alluded to the bonding privilege as only enjoyed by the Canadian people at the good will of our American friends. If he will look at ' Harper's Weekly ' of one or two weeks ago-which can be had in our library-he will find in that journal an article dealing with this question. The writer of that article asks: What is the menace to the good-will now existing between the United States and Great Britain ? And he replies to his own question by saying that the menace which exists to the continued good-will between the American and English nations is the presence of Canada on the North American continent, and until Canada is brought into the American Union by annexation, there will be no assurance of continued friendship and good-will on the part of the American republic towards Great Britain. Or. in other words, the abrogation of the bonding privilege is the weapon which the Amer-

icans are prepared to use against Canada. So long as Canada remains a British colony and a competitor with our American neighbours in trade and commerce, so long will It be a menace to the good-will that should prevail between Great Britain and the United States.
My hon. friend also alluded to the disadvantage of scattered settlement. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is rather late in the day for our lion, friends opposite to bring forward an argument of that kind. If they will look up the political history of this country and the records of this House, they will find that during the regime of the late Mr. Mackenzie, one of the very principles he advocated was that we should in those days build the transcontinental line then contemplated, according as settlement and development required. But our Conservative friends pooh-poohed that argument as a ridiculous one. They did not believe in the utilization of the water stretches; they did not believe in building the railways as the development of the country might call for it ; but they did believe, and subsequently put in practice that belief, that the transcontinental line should be built through from end to end, regardless of whether settlement was sparce or otherwise. And now my hon. friend talks of the disadvantages of sparse settlement. There are undoubtedly great advantages in having settlements close together. There are great advantages in compact communities particularly in a country like the North-west where the privileges and comforts that go with many years of settlement cannot be enjoyed as we enjoy them in the older provinces. Close settlement is advantageous in a variety of ways which I need not enumerate. But in dwelling upon these advantages hon. gentlemen opposite are taking a course directly opposed to that which their party took a few years ago and have accepted identically the platform laid down by the Liberal party in connection with the building of the first transcontinental line. If it were possible for the spirit of the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie to visit these halls he would be astonished to find that his principle and his policy and his platform had been adopted by those who in his lifetime so bitterly denounced him.

gentleman who is interested to the extent that the hon. member for West Toronto is supposed to be interested in the Canadian Pacific Railway, to offer any criticism of this project. Therefore, if the difference in mileage is of any importance the
advantage is decidedly with the government proposition.
Now, the question-may be asked. How is this new railway going to benefit old Ontario V It passes through the newer portion of Ontario, but of what interest is it to old Ontario ? Mr. Speaker, I hope I shall not be considered discourteous if I do not reply in full to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat; and I am sure that he will not consider me so as he knows that I am not familiar with his language. That I regret, as I would very-much- like to be able to reply7 to him in the manner which I have no doubt his speech deserves.
I do not think any apology is necessary for taking part' in this debate. Under ordinary circumstances, after the number of very able speeches that we have listened to on both sides of the House in which this question has been so fully discussed, it would seem as though we might refrain from further consideration of it and be prepared to vote. But, Sir, coming as I do from that portion of the country for whose benefit we are led to believe this great enterprise has to a very great extent been undertaken, I feel that I need not apologize for discussing this question which is to us in the west a very important one. In fact, Sir, I think I am justified in finding fault with the government for the late hour at which they have introduced this Important measure to the House, and I have again to protest against the unseasonable time at which this House was called. It Is true the hon. the Prime Minister has given his reasons for calling the House at that late date- his own illness-but, Sir, if we may judge from what has taken place in regard to the health of that gentleman-and I am as pleased at the improvement as any person here-I think it would have been better for him had he called the House together earlier, for it would seem that between the internal troubles that he has had in the cabinet and his followers, no doubt pressing him as they did, the leader of old who said that he had to sleep on his arms to protect the treasury of this country, it would have been a great deal better for that right hon. gentleman had he called the House at an earlier date. Then he would have been fighting gentlemen on this side of the House who would have fought him face to face and he would have understood exactly7 what they were doing. Therefore that excuse I think is not very good. We protest and have cause to protest at the House being called together at that very unreasonable time-the 12th of March. There is no excuse for it and there is no reason why parliament should be brought together at such a very late day. This important project which had been a matter of discussion all over the country and in the public press ; which was mentioned also in the speech from the Throne ; a proposition equal in importance to any that has been brought to the attention of this parliament or any other parliament since the time of the Cana-

dian Pacific Railway, was not introduced in this House until nearly six months after the calling together of the House. I say that it is treating the opposition most unfairly ; and that the government is deserving of the censure of the people of Canada under the circumstances.
As I said a moment ago there is no portion of the Dominion to which this question is of such interest as to Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. That is very easily understood,' because our success has depended in the past and will in the future depend, largely upon our transportation facilities. Situated as we are, and with the conditions under which we are labouring to procure our livelihood, the success of that country depends on the cheapness with which we can export our products to the markets of the world. Notwithstanding that, however, the people of Manitoba would be quite prepared to accept any further railway construction that may come to them. That remark might be applied not to Manitoba alone but to any other part of the country, for it has been said by the hon. the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) you can put a railway any place, and the people will be glad of it. You might start a railway to the north pole and a certain amount of business would be developed; but the point is-will it be profitable to do so.
The next point is-is this the best proposition which we might expect for the relief, and the benefit, of that great western country ? I have no hesitation in saying that I do not think it is. I shall quote a statement of the Premier, who in his speech said :
Wa consider that it is the duty of all those who sit within these walls by the will of the people, to provide immediate means whereby the products of these new settlers may find an exit to the ocean at the least possible cost.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I claim that this proposal does not fulfil the promise held out to the people in that statement of the Premier. It must have been most conclusively proven to any open mind in this House that this railway is not going to take the products of the settlers of the west to the markets of the world at the least possible cost. In
fact, Sir, it has been shown that it will give no relief in that respect whatever. I may say in passing, that if this appeared to be the best proposal that could be submitted to the people, if this was to my mind a project that is going to give to the settlers the cheapest possible outlet for their products, I for one, would have supported It. But it is not the best, as I shall endeavour as briefly as possible to show, this scheme dees not fulfil, as I said the hope for the promise held out by the Premier. We have heard a great deal about this proposal. We all remember how it was considered in the Railway Committee, and the maimer in which it passed through that body. The leading papers made reference to it before the House met. One of the earliest refrences was made on this subject more than a year ago in the city of Winnipeg, and the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of August 24tli says editorially :
A little more than a year ago, on July 23, 1902, the following article appeared in a Manitoba paper :
The Toronto * Globe ' Hatching Again.
The Toronto ' Globe ' is publishing a series of articles on the railway traffic which for some mysterious reason it choses to believe is so great on Manitoba branch lines that the grain on those lines cannot be hauled out for want of more tracks. It says nothing about the lack of cars and engines which every one here knows was the cause of the blockade.
Those who are familiar with the ways of the ' Globe ' seem to be universally of the opinion that this is not merely a case in which the ' Globe ' is drawing a herring across the track. Looking back over the preliminary symptoms it has manifested for some years, whenever a deal was hatching, they have come to the conclusion that another deal of some sort is in the incubator.
Messrs. .Taffray and Cox, whom Mr. Sifton assisted td get hold of the Crow's Nest coal lands are, it is understood, In control of the Toronto 1 Globe.' Thov are. also mixed up in a western railway transaction with ' Jim Hill ' of the Great Northern and of the Morgan railway group. The question people are now asking is whether there is some Jaffray-Cox deal requiring legislation from parliament, for which the * Globe ' is to pave the way, and which their other domestic employs, Mr. Sifton, is to shove along.
Whereupon Mr. Sifton's loyal organ (the ' Free Press ') promptly asserted that this suspicion was absurd, and that the deal surmised was purely imaginary.
Now Sir, remember that that article was written over a year ago. It was written by a gentleman who at one time held a very high place in the ranks of the Liberal party, and who thoroughly understood what was the meaning of the articles that Were appearing in the ' Globe.' You will observe Sir, that what has transpired in the Railway Committee and in this House, conclusively proves that the prophetic surmise of that experienced gentleman was absolutely correct. We first had a request for a railway charter by the Grand Trunk Railway to run from North Bay to the west.

Then the Liberal members from Quebec, and those associated with the Trans-Canada asserted themselves. Although Mr. Hays had led us to believe and had actually stated, that he had no intention whatever of constructing that road; much to our surprise he came back in a day or two^ and he was perfectly prepared to go to Quebec. Then, Mr. Speaker (Mr. Logan being in the chair) the success of the Quebec gentlemen became apparent to you, and in the interest of your constituents you stood up in the committee, and I well remember that cheerful and sonorous voice of yours demanding of Mr. Hays : Is it your intention to ctirry your railway to the eastern sea-board. If my recollection is correct, Mr. Hays answered : Certainly not. And you, Sir, came out most emphatically and you said :	in
that case I shall oppose your Bill, and you sat down heroically. The size of you Mr. Speaker, towering over Mr. Hays, and the manner in which you asserted yourself, supported as you were by other worthy supporters from the eastern provinces, and no doubt by the Minister of Justice as well-
Oh, no.

Yes, the Minister of Justice came to your assistance Mr. Speaker, and much to our surprise in the committee, back Mr. Hays came the next day and he was ready to swallow the mountain, or for the matter of that, all the mountains between Winnipeg and Moncton. But, what I cannot understand about it is that the Liberal members from Prince Edward Island did not assert themselves. If there had beeh any life in them; if some of the old warriors of the Liberal party from Prince Edward Island in days gone by wei* present, they would ask Mr. Hays : Do you propose to build a tunnel to Prince Edward Island, and Mr. Hays would no doubt say ; Certainly not; but he would return to the committee the next day and he would declare : Why, certainly I will build a tunnel for you. A small matter of that kind did not amount to anything with Mr. Hays, especially when the government would build the tunnel for him as they are building the railroad. I believe that Mr. Hays is the man behind the machine, but no doubt the Minister of Justice saw him and persuaded him to come back to the committee the next iday to tell us that he would build to Moncton. However, as I said before, I do not understand why the Liberals from Prince Edward Island did not get him to promise a tunnel. I do not wonder at Mr. Hays promising to build through Quebec, or through New Brunswick, or up to the North Pole, for it was quite immaterial to him so long as the country was going to do the building, and to give him the road to manage for his benefit, although we may have it in fifty years from now if it does'nt pay the Grand Trunk Railway to keep it any longer. Of course, Mr. Speaker, these few
trifling matters were arranged between^you and the gentlemen behind the scenes,~ and so six months after the House met-against which delay I again protest-we had this scheme launched on an unsuspecting public. Well, we have heard a good deal about it for the last three weeks in this House, and we are going to hear more about it for some time, and when we get to the country we will hear more about it still. It is astonishing the amount of information we will be able to give to the electors from both sides of politics, when the proper time comes. But, perhaps the most astute part of the whole thing was the speech of the Minister of Finance when he told us that it was going to cost $13,000,000.
What about the Prime Minister ?

Well, the Prime Minister said that too, but the Minister of Finance with his actuary settled the whole thing. However, that $13,000,000 story has been so exploded, that like the bonding privilege we have not heard much about it recently. But, Sir, fallacy of the calculation was so apparent that I did not expect it from the Minister of Finance, because 1 have a good deal of respect for him, and 1 did not expect that a gentleman occupying his position would try to delude the people of the country. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have had an actuary to work also on these figures, and I propose to engraft them into my statement so that they may be handed down to posterity, bound in that volume containing the speeches of this debate, which I have no doubt will be published so that in years to come posterity may see the fallaciousness of the men who now occupy the treasury benches. I will estimate that this government road from Winnipeg to Moncton will cost $48,900 per mile, which the Grand Trunk Railway in the little book which has been published by them says is the cost of the Intercolonial Railway, and therefore the 1,800 miles from Winnipeg to Moncton at $48,900 a mile, will, according to my actuary, cost in the neighbourhood of $88,020,000. There are 1,000 miles of prairie section at $13,000 per mile, making $13,000,000, and 625 miles of mountain section at $30,000 per mile, making $18,750,000; or a total of $119,770,000. Add interest during construction, $10,080,450, and at the end of the Construction period you have a total of $129,850,450. Add interest for seven years, $29,885,603, or another total of $159,736,053. Add three years interest if the company do not pay any actual in the, three years-and I do not expect they will, and I do not believe that any man in this House expects, they will when they are not bound to; that would be $14,374,357; or a total of $174,110,410.
In making up these figures, Sir, I have procured the services of as accurate an actuary as did the Minister of Justice ; and

the Minister of Finance, no doubt, associated with the Minister of Justice. All that the gentleman asked was that his name should not be divulged owing to the position he occupies ; but he could vouch for the accuracy of these figures, which I place on ' Hansard,' and I defy contradiction of them. That is the position the people of this country will find themselves in if this railroad Is carried to the position where the government seem to think they are going to take it.
Mr. Speaker, the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not want this scheme. They showed it in every move they made before the Railway Committee. They are not anxious) to get it even as a present, as my hon. friend says. What they did want they have got. They wanted a guarantee of their bonds to carry them across the profitable prairies of the west, where they did not need it and should not have got it, at any rate so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned. They have also got a guarantee of the mountain section. That, Sir, is what they sought when they came to this parliament; and what they did not want the government of this country has proposed to give them for nothing, and to saddle this country with the enormous debt that I have mentioned.
Now, where is the business of that railroad going during the time this road is under construction ?-because if this Bill passes this House, in one year from the time it passes, the company, if they exert themselves to the extent that they should be able to, can have 500 or 000 miles of the producing portion constructed across the prairies. Before the government have the surveys made of the eastern division, they will have the total length of the line across the prairies completed. Where is the produce of that constructed line going ? Has there been any arrangement made by the government ? Have they placed anything in that contract to say that the produce shall pass through a Canadian channel ? There is no clause of that kind. There is nothing to prevent the company sending the freight just where they intend to send it, and that is across the American boundary to their own American system. It lias been reported in the papers that they have acquired the Wisconsin Central Railway, which brings them to the city of Duluth or within a few miles of it. It is well understood who is associated with the gentlemen who have managed to manipulate this matter through this House-Mr. Hill, who was, I think, connected with the Crow's Nest Pass matter, in which fortunes were made for a number of people ; and it would be very easy to make arrangements with that gentleman whereby, the business which the Grand Trunk Company procure in the prairies of Manitoba and the North-west Territories will pass over his system to Superior City, whence it will be shipped to Chicago. They will take 316
the wheat to the lakes and carry it across to Georgian bay ports, and pass it on over the Grand Trunk system to Portland or wherever they see fit to take it; and there is no provision in this contract to prevent them doing so. I contend that some clause should be inserted to provide that during the time of construction the produce of the prairies shall pass through Canadian channels, and I think it is the duty of the opposition to see that a clause to that effect is inserted in the Bill.
We all remember the action of the Liberal party when they gained power in the province of Manitoba. One of the first things they did was to make an arrangement to bring an American system of railways into that province. They held an election on it. They said : We have made an arrangement that is going to be very beneficial to the people of Manitoba. They had a portion of the line built, and when the legislature forced the premier to lay on the Table of the House what that arrangement was, what do you suppose was the great concession they had obtained ? That the Americah railway would not charge any more than the Canadian Pacific Railway charged. That was the great concession the Liberals in the province of Manitoba gave to the farmers of that province for saddling them with a debt of close on $1,000,000, and they had absolutely no control of rates. However, when the Conservative party removed them from power, they very readily got rid of that incubus, and succeeded in buying back that portion of the Americau system for the people of Manitoba. They have leased that to a Canadian system, and it has been a success from that day to the present. We have the Liberals in Ottawa introducing legislation into this House, which, if they succeed in carrying it through, will saddle Manitoba and the North-west Territories with another system leading into the United States. That is what the Grand Trunk Railway Company wanted when they came to this House, and that is what they have got; and there is where the business is going during the ten years that you will be constructing your railroad. I say, Mr. Speaker, and I speak with some experience, that the railway between Moncton and Winnipeg-if it should ever be completed-will not be completed inside of ten years and during that time this system which you are bonusing to carry the products of that western country down to the United States will have become so well established that you will have great difficulty-if you ever do it-to bring it back to Canadian channels. The grain will go to Duluth and the ordinary frieght will go down over the Grand Trunk Railway to Chicago.
Let me give a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to the consideration of this line which the government is going to build-what the ex-



Minister of Railways and Canals calls the lean portion-and they will find it very lean before they get through with it, politically as well as commercially. The Canadian Pacific Railway is built, some people say, too close to the shores of Lake Superior, and this will be a disadvantage in case of trouble with the Americans. Well, that is not a matter worth mentioning. But the building of a line close to the shores of Lake Superior has been a great benefit to the Canadian Pacific Railway. It has given them several coaling stations. Jackfish, Fort William, and another place, Peninsula Harbour, I think it is, are ports where they bring in large quantities of coal and freight and supply the railway system up and down on the north shore of Lake Superior. But what port will this road have at which to procure anything of the kind ? The government will have to haul all that freight and other stores and material back to this proposed line, 150 miles north of Lake Superior. Then, what is the arrangement about building this branch from Port Arthur back ? Who builds that ? The Grand Trunk Railway will have that, and if at any [DOT]time there should be any trouble, who will own the branch that will carry the grain from Winnipeg to the waters of the lake ? That is another question which has not been considered as thoroughly as it should. I say that this road to be built by the Dominion government will be at a very great disadvantage indeed, being built so far (back, during the time of construction, and even after it lias been completed. How or where is the company going to get its coal ? Every one who knows anything about it can readily understand what it will cost to handle coal two or three times in order to get it back 150 miles away from the lakes as against the Canadian Pacific Railway, which lias three or four coaling stations along that lake. And not alone that, but if any trouble should arise, that very important portion of this road will be held by the Grand Trunk Railway themselves. Then we come to the question of the cost of the road. That, I think, is a very important part, or at least it is going to be with the people of the North-west, because the cost of that road is going to come very largely into consideration. I want to be fair, and I propose to quote from the speech of the hou. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who was put up, as the mouthpiece of the government, to reply to the ex-Minister of Railways anl Canals, and the government is consequently bound by his utterances in this respect, and none of the ministers have repudiated them. On page 8481 of ' Hansard,' you will find these words :
No road can claim to be a first-class road with grades more than ont-half per cent or twenty-six feet to the mile. Tn the construction of this short line and in the construction of the line from Quebec to Winnipeg it should

be an absolute condition that the road should be first-class in point of grades, in point of construction and in point of weight of rails. The rails should not be less than ninety-pound rails, * and the grades should not be more than four-tenths per cent, and if these conditions are complied with this road will compete with a water-route or anything else.
I would like the govemmefit to produce a contract from some practical contractor on the information given to this House. X would like some practical contractor to be asked what he would construct a railway of that kind for. When the hon. gentleman speaks of building a road like that for $28,000 per mile, he shows his total ignorance of the subject. I say that we cannot get any practical railway man who has any reputation or any money to lose, who will agree to build a railway such as that for $28,000 per mile-no, nor for fifty thousand a mile. I question if you can get any man to build such a road as. has been described by the mouthpiece of the government, for $60,000 per mile. I speak with some experience. I spent some years in railway construction. I was a contractor myself ; I spent two years upon the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as assistant to Mr. M. J. Haney, building a portion of the road which the contractor had failed to complete between Rat Portage and Winnipeg-building a portion of the road that cost, not $26,000, not $50,000, hut a great deal of it $85,000 per mile.
Ninety pound rails ?

No, and no such grades and curves as the mouthpiece of the government says this road must have. Why, the thing is an absurdity. No man) who has a reputation, no man who knows anything at all about It, no man who has any money to lose, would agree, upon the information laid before this House, to build such a road even for $60,000 per mile. It cannot be done. We have to look at the cost of other railways. Here is the Intercolonial Railway, which cost $53,000 per mile and over, the Canadian Pacific Railway, which cost $52,000 per mile, the Canadian Pacific Railway on the north shore of Lake Superior. which cost $50,000 per mile, the Canada Atlantic Railway, which cost $50,000 l>er mile, the Grand Trunk Railway, which cost $106,000 per mile. Are any of these such roads as the mouthpiece of the government says this road shall be ? No. Why, the mouthpiece of the government, this prospective minister, says that the grades on those other roads will not do at all. They are away behind the times, totally unfit to meet the present requirements of the country, and this road is to be built up to the latest requirements. Mark what I tell you, if you build such a road as that between Winnipeg and Moncton It will cost nearer $60,000 than $28,000.
What will it cost to buy the Canadian Pacific Railway ?

That Is a point I propose to touch on a little later. As was shown by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), the Grand Trunk Railway has paid only one and a quarter per cent on its capital. It lias never paid a dividend on its ordinary stock of about $110,000,000, although its prospectus promised the exact figure of 11} per cent, to say nothing of the $74,000,000 or $75,000,000 which it owes the people of Canada. Even the actuaries of the present day cannot figure it out any more nicely than does the prospectus of the Grand Trunk . They were to make 11} per cent. And the Grand Trunk lias 3,142 miles. It has paid a dividend of about $800 per mile. That road runs through a first-class country, Ontario and down to Chicago. It owes $202,000,000, and it manages to pay dividends on only one-quarter of the said debt, or $800 per mile. Yet it is expected to pay interest on $28,000 a mile, at 3 per cent, which would make $840 per mile-more, mark you, than it paid on its mileage last year. Or on say $50,000 per'mile-and it will be a great deal nearer $50,000 than it is $28,000-they would pay $1,500 per mile. Now, I would like any man on that side of the House to show how the people of Manitoba and the North-west are going to get the relief that the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) was apparently pleading for, through the building of this road under these conditions. Sir, it is an impossibility-it cannot be expected, and it will not be done.
Would it be given by buying the Canadian Pacific Railway line around the north shore of Bake Superior ?

I will deal with that in due order. In the meantime, I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) that I am prepared to discuss that phase of it with him here or in any other place he may select to have it done. Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sif-ton) with all his astuteness-and he has no superior, no equal, in fact among the members of this House in that respect-could not figure out a better rate on this new line than 10.85 cents per bushel on wheat from Winnipeg to the seaboard, and in making this rate he was most unfair taking what the member for Peel designated a bargain day rate between Kansas City and Chicago to get even that rate. But look at the rate that exists to-day. From Winnipeg to Port Arthur, six cents per bushel ; Port Arthur to Depot Harbour, one cent per bushel ; Depot Harbour to Montreal, 2} cents per bushel, or a total from Winnipeg to Mont-treal of 9} cents per bushel. Thus, the rate actually charged to-day is 1.60 cents per bushel less than the very best that the Minister of the Interior could figure out as possible on this new line. This applied to the Minister of Agriculture's figures, 200,000,000 bushels, would make the saving to
the farmers of Manitoba and the Northwest of $2,200,000 by the use of the present route as compared with what would be charged if this new line of the government were in use and were carrying the grain at the rates estimated by the Minister of the Interior.
Now, is this project going to work out to the interests of the people in Manitoba ? Is it going to be a benefit to the grain growers of that province, and will it give them relief in respect to transportation facilities ? We find, as I have shown, that if grain is carried over it, it will cost 1.60 per bushel more than is charged by the rail and water route at the present time. By the time this new road is constructed, ten years hence, it is hard to say how much lower the freights by rail and water will be. It has been shown in this House over and over again_(hat, as rapidly as the railroad rates fall those on the rail and water route go down equally. If the Minister of the Interior could do no better than he did, and if this road is being built as a grain-carrying road
Was that not a winter rate entirely ?

The minister's quotation was on the all-rail route as against the rail and water route. He estimated from Port Arthur, and he has no roads to Port Arthur and there is no provision made for a railroad to that point under control of the government. If they are to get to Port Arthur it will be by the grace of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk will charge what they please. This is an all-rail rate ; that is what he wanted
Certainly.

If that is the best that can be done,' this is not a proposition that would recommend itself to the people of Manitoba and the North-west. It will not give them the relief that has been spoken about. As a colonization road, to open up a new portion of the country as a means of creating more railway competition in Manitoba and out into the territories, and as a means of affording railway facilities for those who have none now, why, of course it will be acceptable. Such railways are always acceptable, one or twenty of them. Now, what is the local trade that we may look for on that north shone of Lake Superior ?
Christmas trees.

Yes, as the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) suggests, Christmas trees and woodpeckers, as it was stated by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) in speaking of the immigration agent of the Ontario government. There is a crop of these almost all the time. The building up of any other business, however, is problematical. The possibility of settling these

lands while thousands, hundreds of thousands and millions of acres of good land in Manitoba and the North-west remain untilled, is very remote indeed. I do not believe that any man would be the friend of his son or his neighbour and advise that son or that neighbour to go into these wilds to make a home when he might direct him to the prairies of the west. But, suppose that the timber of which the hon. gentleman speaks is in existence to the north of us here, why should settlers be sent in there at this late date in the history of Canada to destroy that timber by cutting it down and burning it and so losing it to the country ? Our timber, if of merchantable quality, is the most valuable asset we have in Canada to-day. Why, then, should it be burned up and destroyed, it must be if settlers are to go in there and make farms for themselves ? The probability of these lands being settled by people who will make a business for the road is very remote indeed. It seems to me strange that the government of Ontario did not discover these lands years ago, especially strange when you consider how near they are to the city of Toronto. It is also strange to me why the government of Ontario did not give the volunteers their grants in these valuable agricultural lands instead of placing them, as they did, upon the rocks a mile square apart and with the pine timber reserved.
Where there was any.

Yes, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) remarks, where there was any. When they wished to recompense these men for the sacrifices they had made it is strange that they did not give them these agricultural lands. It looks very much-and subsequent events have indicated the same thing-as if all this was due to the approach of an election. We do not hear so much about it now, at any rate. I could quote from page 23 of the pamphlets that the Grand Trunk Railway has issued and sent to members of the House the description of the country and of the business they expect to do there. As there will be no business done there possibly within the life of the present generation, what benefits are we likely to derive, we people in the west, from this road passing through the wilderness such as that will be at such an enormous cost as will be involved in the construction and operation of this road.
Now, Sir, I have shown that you cannot construct that road at any such price as the government has intimated. No man knows the distance, no man in this House can tell the cost per mile, no man can tell where it is to be located, and no man can tell what benefit it is going to be to the people, especially to the people of the west. Under these circumstances, why this hurry, why this anxiety ? After sitting here for seven years, what has occurred to make this departure necessary ? We are Mr. BOYD.
told that there was great congestion in that country in 1901 and 1902, but the government did nothing then. Now, Mr. Speaker, when there is no likelihood of congestion this year, or possibly next year, owing to the great increase in the rolling stock of these two railways, why this hysteria on the part of the government ? Well, some hon. gentlemen say that time won't wait. I think the extract I read from that paper printed over a year ago explains the whole reason, as showing the manner in which the Grand Trunk Railway Company expects to handle this business. The whole question is wrapped up in uncertainty. There has been nothing but * perhaps ' and ' ifs ' presented to this House as reasons for voting away $174,000,000. That seems to he the only certain thing that we know in regard to it. According to the statement of the mouthpiece of the government who was put up to reply to the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, there is no possibility that the government will get any return for their money, there is no possibility of any lowering of rates, in fact it is almost certain that no lowering of rates will take place under these conditions.
Now, Sir, I have always been a believer in the extension of the Intercolonial across the continent, and I still believe that it would be a governor of the rates, and as such it would certainly be a great benefit to all the people of the country. It is bound to be a great benefit to the railway itself. If it is removed from political control-and it will have to be removed from political control, it can be removed from political control-when that is done, I am satisfied that if this road were constructed across the continent it would be a great national benefit. In this connection I may say that I would like to see a branch built to the Hudson's bay. When this road reaches across the continent the country may well look for some control of rates ; for some relief from high freight rates. I am not prepared to go so far as the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) and to purchase the whole railroad system of this country. At the same time, I would like to see the Intercolonial cross this continent, and if that proved a success, then the extension of the principle of government ownership would follow in the natural course of events. Now the proposition of the leader of the opposition is the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Georgian bay, and I am in favour of that idea. But what may we expect from that ? We have absolute control of rates in the province of Manitoba, we control the rates over almost every portion of that province, and in a few years I expect the extension of the Canadian Northern into the Territories, when the same control will I presume apply. It has been shown repeatedly in this House that one cent a bushel carries grain across Lake Superior, then when it

comes to the Georgian bay and passes into the hands of a government road, any person will readily see that we have in that case almost absolute control of the carriage across the lakes. Competition will keep the rate at the lowest possible point and in that way the people would have almost absolute control of rates. You can readily see what benefit that will be to the farmers in Manitoba and to the people in the east, because the managers of the Intercolonial in that case will be able to say where the freight should go ; and they will take it undoubtedly to Canadian ports, to Montreal in the summer season, and to Quebec and the maritime province ports in winter.
We are told by the Minister of the Interior that the Intercolonial Railway has not paid in the past. Why has it not paid ? The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals told us when he was at the head of that department, and he was loudly applauded by the hon. gentlemen who then sat around him, why it did not pay. If I charged, said he, the same rates as are charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, I could make one or two millions a year. It has not paid because the rates have been low. Another reason why it has not paid is because it is located, as I understand, in Montreal where it receives no through freight from any railroad ; or if it receives any, it is a very small amount, and practically it has to depend upon its local freight business ; what it may pick up in the city of Montreal, and along its line. When you come to carry that railroad to the shores of the inland seas, and place it in a position to compete with traffic across the lakes, when you place that railroad in a position to receive a great portion of the business from Manitoba and the North-west Territories, then you will find a magnificent business for that road ; you will be doing good to the west and good to the east, and you will be building up your whole system. I think that will mean a great deal more business for the lower provinces, a great deal more business for the winter ports in which the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) is so deeply interested. Because you cannot carry wheat down there, and if you are not going to carry wheat on your proposed Grand Trunk Pacific, what business are you going to do ? I am told on very good authority that the average freight movement over the Canadian Pacific Railway north of Lake Superior, is one train and a half per day.
Well, if that is all that the Canadian Pacific Railway has now in the carriage of freight, then when the Grand Trunk Pacific is running around, as it will, by Duluth and Chicago, what are you going to carry over your road, even admitting that the great increase which we expect and hope for takes place ? Where is the business in ordinary freight that is to accumulate around our winter ports ?
You cannot haul wheat; that has been conclusively shown. Therefore, I claim that by constructing this road to the Georgian bay-and a modern road 380 miles long could be constructed with easy grades, a road on which you would be able to haul trains of 60 or 70 cars-you would be doing, something that would be profitable to the people of the west, profitable to the Intercolonial, and profitable to the winter ports. That road would be bound to secure business, and I am satisfied that when the proposal of the leader of the opposition has been studied and weighed and considered by the people of Canada, it will appeal to their better reason. The closing words of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) were that no road without a paying connection is any good. The Intercolonial Railway has not a paying connection at the present time, but it would have a paying connection if it were extended to the Georgian bay and thence on across the continent. In order to support tile position that was taken by the hon. leader of the opposition, I wish here to quote a portion of an interview with Mr. Meighen, president of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, one of the largest shippers of heavy freight from the province of Manitoba. This interview was given on August 6tli, before the proposal of the leader of the opposition had been submitted to this House, and it bears out almost to the letter what the leader of the opposition said. This gentleman has had as much experience in this matter as any man in Canada, because the whole business of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company is a matter of freights, the grinding of flour and the passing of their goods on to the market. This interview appeared in the St. John ' Telegraph ' on August 6th, and is headed ' Allrail route no good for grain.' It is as follows
You will never bring the products of Manitoba or the North-west, either by the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk Pacific, or an all-rail route around the north of Lake Superior to our Canadian ports ; neither will you ever bring but a small portion by our Canadian canals, east of the Soo.
These are the words of Robert Meighen, president of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, who arrived in St. John yesterday, to attend the annual meeting of the New Brunswick Railway Company.
Mr. Meighen is emphatic in his declaration that the lakes must be taken into account in any scheme of transportation for the grain of the great west. Only a portion, he says, of the products of our western prairies will ever be handled through Canadian ports by an all-rail route north of Lake Superior, or even through the canal system.
What are needed, he says, are double-track railways from Montreal to Georgian bay. and ample elevator space there to store grain for shipment by rail to St. John and Halifax-when navigation is closed to the St. Lawrence. If wheat is purchased in Brandon, or west of that point after October 25, the shipper cannot get it through the canals. He has only two alternatives-he can store it in the elevator, or send

it forward to Fort William, and from there to Buffalo, and on by rail to an American winter port. For it can be taken from Fort William to Buffalo until early in December,
Now, said Mr. Meighen, what Canada needs is facilities on Georgian bay for receiving grain, and railways to carry it on via Montreal to St. John and Halifax. It could be shipped from Fort William to Georgian bay ports up to the 12th of December, and elevators there could be filled to provide trainloads of grain for the whole winter, to be shipped from our own winter ports. At present a large amount of our grain goes by way of Buffalo.
You can get ports on Georgian bay that will give you a grade to Montreal over which eighty cars of grain could be hauled in a single train.
With sufficient elevator capacity at Georgian bay ports, and railway from there to Montreal, you can cut out Buffalo, and give the Canadian grain trade to Canadian ports. You can freight wheat across the lake from Fort William to Georgian bay ports for one cent, and from there to Montreal for three and a half cents, or less, per bushel winter and summer.
Our canals are closed for six months in. the year. With elevators at Georgian bay you can store there all the grain that is too late to be forwarded by the St. Lawrence route, and with proper railway facilities from those elevators to Montreal you can send this grain on to St. John and Halifax.
' When the foregoing is accomplished,' said Mr. Meighen, ' our western prairies will ship their products by an all-Canadian route, and only a portion of them will ever he handled through Canadian ports under our canal system or an all-rail route north of Lake Superior.'
Mr. Meighen is very emphatic in his declaration that Canadian ports should get the western trade in winter as well as in summer. St. John and Halifax, he says, are a part of Canada, and their claims deserve support.
Asked if he favoured extending the Intercolonial Railway to Georgian bay, Mr. Meighen replied that he had no suggestion to offer on that point, further than what he had already stated. Railways and elevators were needed, and should be in some way provided.
This is the statement of a gentleman who has possibly given that aspect of the transportation question more consideration than any other man in Canada, and, as I have said, this statement was made some days, or even weeks, before the proposition of the leader of the opposition was laid before this House. I think, Sir, that these are words which should recommend themselves to the people of this country ; and I believe that they will. I have also a quotation from Mr. Ashdown, who in Winnipeg said :
I, personally, would have preferred the government not only to have owned the eastern section, but owned and operated the whole.
And Mr. Ashdown is one of the gentlemen quoted by the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) during his remarks.
Then, here is the opinion of Mr. Fisher, who for many years was president of the Liberal Association of Manitoba and who lias stood high in the ranks of the Liberal party. He is a Liberal to-day, a gentleman who is no political friend of the Conservative party, and whom I have found op-Mr. BOYD.
posed to me in nearly every political campaign I have been engaged in in Manitoba. Here is what he says :
I confess I entertain some doubt as to whether the proposed route wil'l be a valuable competitor in the near future, owing to the location. What Manitoba needs above all things is the shortest and cheapest route to Lake Superior. I doubt if much of our wheat for a long time to come, will be carried allrail. That is. I doubt if for a long time to come any road can afford to carry it all-rail. It strikes me that the proposed line is so far north as not to give so favourable a route as either the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern. Perhaps the most valuable addition to our transportation facilities at the present time would he the double tracking of the Canadian Pacific Railway ito Lake Superior, because It Is, I believe, the Shortest exclusive Canadian route to the great lakes, and will continue for many years to come the great funnel through which our grain will pass outward to the east ; and my doubt Is that whether with a line so far north, the cost of operating through a country little known and in which the local traffic is not a measurable quantity the cost will not be so heavy as to make the rates excessively high.
There Is the opinion of a gentleman who is no friend of the Conservative party, no friend of the leader of the opposition ; a gentleman who has spent a quarter of a century in the province of Manitoba ; a man of ability and of intelligence and discernment ; a gentleman who was selected by tbe Greenway government to represent them on the expedition that went to the Hudson bay ; that is the opinion of that gentleman on the western portion of the scheme of the leader of the opposition. I have given yon the opinion on the eastern portion of that scheme, by one of the largest shippers In Canada. We cannot overlook these opinions. There is no place in the Dominion of Canada where the people are giving, day by day, tbe question of transportation such consideration as they do in the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba generally. When you get such an opinion as that from a gentleman who is not a political Mend of ours, it ought to cause the government supporters to pause. I fear they will not be impressed by anything that might be said from this side of the House, but an opinion such as this is worthy of their serious consideration. A great deal has been said about the routing of freight over the government road. Well, if you want to control the routing and the rating retain tire railroad in your own hands. That is the only way to do it. Not a gentleman on the other side of the House has yet proven that the Grand Trunk Railway is bound to send one dollar's worth of its freight to any eastern port in this country.
What we in the west want is cheaper freight rates, especially for our cattle and our grain. I claim that the proposition submitted by the government will not secure that for us. I claim that under the conditions on which this road is to be constructed

the settlers of the west cannot hope for cheaper rates. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railroad is to be capitalized west of Winnipeg at $56,660 per mile. That capitalization is as high as the present capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The capitalization of the Canadian Northern Railway, controlled by the Manitoba government is $12,500 a mile. How can you charge cheap freight rates on a road capitalized so high as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ? And who is going to get that $20,000,000 of common stock. No one has yet told us where that portion of the $56,000 per mile is going. I have no doubt that is some of the watered stock that the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) referred to. I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to lay before the House my views on this subject. I am opposed, Mr. Speaker to this scheme which you are largely instrumental in giving to this country. The leader of the government pleaded for immediate relief for the traffic of the west. We (will get no immediate relief from this road, which will not be constructed for the next ten years at least. The member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) spoke for an hour and the only advantage he could claim for the road was that it would give additional railway facilities and consequently competition. It has not been shown yet and It cannot be shown that this road will give cheaper freight rates. If you go ahead with this enterprise you will involve the couptry in enormous expense. That expenditure being such a heavy burden on the country it will prevent us grappling with other schemes which are an absolute necessity for Canada.
On thei other hand the scheme submitted by the leader of the opposition will commence to pay immediately. If we acquire the Canada Atlantic Railway and make it a portion of the Intercolonial Railway, it will commence to pay at once. The plan of the government is uncertain as to its>
completion, and it is bound to be expensive. By our plan we will own the road, but by the government plan the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway owns the road and have control of the rates. But, Sir, there is one thing certain about the government scheme, and that is its enormous cost. It would seem as if the government and those who were pressing them on are more anxious as to what -the results will be at the approaching elections than they are as to what benefits their project will confer on the people of the North-west and Canada generally. The member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) told us that no one on this side had given information as to the cost of the proposal of the leader of the opposition, and the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) followed him in that assertion. Well, if they had listened to the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) they would have had full information on that point, but when a member
on this side speaks hon. gentlemen opposite get out. They don't want any information or any enlightenment. When one of their own side speaks, they pile into the chamber and start hammering their desks..
We are here now.
Yes, there are a quorum of you here, but if you could do with less you would not be here.
My hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) is not very successful amongst his own friends.
It is Friday night, we all know what that means.
So it is on this side.

Well, I am making the same retort as was made by the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). Now, Sir. we already have the Intercolonial Railway from Halifax to Montreal and the distances and cost involved in the scheme proposed by the leader of the opposition have been given by the member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) as follows :

342 miles, with equipment	 12,000,000

at $40,000	   4,160,000

at $30,000	 12,780,000
