Against this you have the government project, which I have shown will cost $174,000,000. With the plan of the hon. leader of the opposition we give immediate relief to the people of the west; we give the people of Canada immediate control of rates not only in the west, but in the east ; we give busine-ss to the Intercolonial Railway, and we make the property profitable. For my part I want to see the intercolonial extended further than is proposed. I hope the day is not far distant when we shall see it across this continent controlling the rates. There is no question about the success that is bound to attend this proposition. Before we leave this House, we shall very likely be able to bring the government around to our way of thinking. I am prepared to make this challenge:	Let this House submit
the proposal of the leader of the opposition and the proposal of the leader of the government to three or five of the best expert, practical railway men in America ; and if they do not say that the proposal of the leader of the opposition is a better solution of the problem -than the one that has been submitted by the government, they can have my support. But they are not" likely

to receive for their proposal the endorsement of any practical and experienced railroad men.
I claim that this government! has no mandate from the people on this question. It was never discussed by the people and they have had no opportunity of expressing their opinion upon it. I claim that they should have an opportunity of expressing an opinion upon it before it is made law, and I do not think the opposition will be fulfilling their duty in this House if they permit this measure to pass until the people of this country have that opportunity. If my views are entertained in the councils of the opposition, they will not permit this measure to pass in the form in which the government expect to carry it, regardless of what time it may take in order to give the public an opportunity of expressing an opinion upon it. It is an enormous expenditure and an enormous undertaking- an undertaking that very few people in this country know anything about, that very few men in this House know anything about; and before asking us to vote such an enormous amount of money to build a railroad through what is practically a wilderness, so far as we are able to learn, and thereby leave It impossible for us to undertake the many other great enterprises required for the benefit of the country for possibly fifty years to come, it is the duty of the government to give the people of this1 country an opportunity of expressing their opinion upon it. If the government and their supporters are as sanguine as they claim to be, and as much in earnest as they pretend to be when applauding their speakers, they should be willing to say : We are so certain of the merits of this scheme that we will let it stand, and after the session we will go to the country and fight it out. As the bon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) said, let us all act as Canadians, and let us work in the best interests of the country. Sir, I am prepared to say if the government will submit this question to the people, and the people say yes, it is the best proposal, and we want you to go ahead with it, we on this side of the House will say, all right, we will join with you and push it to a success as fast as we possibly can ; and w-e will not act as the Liberal party acted during the time of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We will not decry the road and the country through which it passes, and make it embarrassing for the people who are carrying on the work, to finance it ; but you will find the opposition, if we are in opposition, after the people have an opportunity of expressing their opinion, giving your great scheme, as it would then be, but" as it is not now, our full approval and support.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, there is no place in the Dominion of Canada where this matter has such vital interest
for the people as it has in the west. I have made a study of this question to the best of my ability, as every other man in the west has done. Our way of making money, in the meantime, at least, and our way of spreading money through eastern Canada, has largely been by raising and shipping wheat. We have spent throughout Canada between $35,000,000 and $40,000,000 which we received for last year's crop, and^ we spent nearly as much the year before ; and that money has been realized largely from the wheat that we have raised. We will do a good deal more in the future. This is a matter that the government should think very seriously about, and before this measure is made law, I trust that they will satisfy themselves that they are acting in a manner that is going to be in the best interests of the people of the west and of the whole of Canada. I have no hesitation in saying that their scheme is not, in my opinion, going to give immediate relief. I do not believe it is going to give relief at any time in the matter of the haulage of that wheat which has made the millions which we have circulated in the country and which will make the millions Which we hope to circulate throughout Canada in the future. A very serious responsibility rests upon the people who are governing this country at the present time, as a false step now may have very* serious results in the future.
I have said that I am not in favour of the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), who proposes that we should take charge of all the railroads of this country ; but I am in favour of the extension of the government system, and I propose, Mr. Speaker, with your permission, to close my remarks by moving an amendment to the amendment. I beg to move :
That all the words in the amendment after the word ' policy ' in the third line be left out and the following substituted : 'of extending and developing our system of government railway and of placing the operation thereof entirely beyond the influence of party politics.'

At this late hour, Mr. Speaker, I shall take up but a very few moments ; but before speaking to the subject, I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite what authority they have for constantly taunting us with dissenting and disagreeing among ourselves. Evidently, in their case the wish is father to the thought. But let me inform these hon. gentlemen that when, by any chance, dissensions or disagreements do take place on this side, either a resignation occurs or is asked for. We are not given to backbiting or going out on strike, and in that respect the present cabinet is in striking contrast with its predecessor. The present cabinet has completely changed the aspect of Canadian government and Canadian public life. The low standard of public life, the unseemly strife, the undermining, the

corruption and all that sort of thing which formerly prevailed, and of which the last Conservative administration was so striking an example, have all disappeared and been replaced by a spirit of confidence and honour among public men and an aggressive policy on the part of the government, which command the admiration and confidence of the country. As this debate goes on from day to day the policy of the government gains in strength. The reasons given in support of that policy are in marked contrast with the chaotic argument furnished by the opposition, who seem to have no idea of union among themselves except the union of opposition, who sieem to be guided by no particular principles, who lay down contradictory policies, and who fail utterly to agree, not only in their attacks on the government policy, but in their support of the position taken by their own leader. As these lion, gentlemen address the House one after another, we are more and more at a loss to know what it is they really do want, except to get back into office at any price and by any possible means.
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to go into any details regarding the cost of the road, because that has been thoroughly gone into by speakers on both sides who have preceded me. But I wish to put myself on record as thoroughly and as strongly in favour of the project submitted to us by the government. This road proposed by the government will pass from the Atlantic to the Pacific all through Canadian soil.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that he is at thie Atlantic when he reaches Moncton ?
Certainly ; Moncton is on the Atlantic.
I am afraid it will be a poor ocean port.

I say that this road will go from the Atlantic to the Pacific on Canadian soil and will serve a threefold purpose. In the first place, it will be a colonization road, which will promote settlement and local development, passing from the north-west to the south-east. Through New Brunswick it will open up. a most fertile country, heretofore undeveloped, and in doing this, it will not parallel the Intercolonial Railway, but, on the contrary, by developing new resources which have hitherto lain dormant and thus increasing traffic generally, it will be an advantage to the Intercolonial Railway. Through the province of Quebec it will develop magnificent water powers and mineral regions, which will, in all probability, in the comparatively near future, become manufacturing centres of this great continent. Going through Ontario, it will develop an immense extent of arable and timber land and mineral resources of the extent of which we can now form no adequate idea. Through 316J
Manitoba and the territories it will go over the old Mackenzie route, now recognized to be the one which should have originally been taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and will pass through a section of country which is the home of the finest hard wheat in the world. Then, in British Columbia it will develop a country which is blessed with a climate and soil and resources that are unequalled. It will be a national road, which, by creating a certain amount of interdependence among the provinces, will strengthen confederation. It will be further a national highway and a link in the commerce around the world. Wo all know the extent of the commerce upon the Orient that has been developed by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and we may reasonably expect a much greater development to take place in that commerce on the completion of this road.
So far as the agreement made by the government with the Grand Trunk Pacific is concerned, I cannot see how a firmer and tighter contract could have been made. I do not see how the interests of the people could have Iveen better safeguarded than they are by this agreement. In fact, what strikes me is that the contract is such a hard and fast one, looking at it from the standpoint of the people, that I am surprised at the company accepting it. In every possible respect the interests of the public have been guarded. That cannot be said of the proposition submitted by the hon. leader of the opposition. What he would have us do is to buy up the existing railways which are running through a developed country, buy up roads that have already been subsidized by the government. On the contrary, our idea was to go on and develop a new country, almost a new Canada. with resources in timber, mines and agriculture as yet unknown and undeveloped, which, when completed will more than ever emphasize the (act that we are a growing young nation. Lying to the south of us is a nation with a population fourteen times our own. The constant tendency of our young men is to leave home and engage in various occupations in that country. When our policy is carried out, as I say, it will enlarge our working territory, it will increase our advantages in every possible way, it will keep our young men at home, and will develop the country that we are all so proud of. Of course, it is absolutely necessary that a policy of some sort should be announced by the opposition, and we have had one presented, composed of all sorts of immature propositions such as might be presented by any irresponsible person utterly incapable of accomplishing or carrying out what he proposed. The policy of the government has been described as a hybrid policy. It would be fair to characterize the policy of the opposition as the same.
Only more so.

Yes, probably, a little more so. Now, in all seriousness, several members of the opposition have asked for an appeal to the country on these two rival policies. X have no doubt whatever that, if the truth were known, they, in their hearts are not honest in their expressions of opinion. To a very great extent. they agree with us in our line of action, and it is only party exigencies and not patriotic motives that influence them in the course that they have taken. I heard with great pleasure the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) express the wish that the young men of our country should be better and more properly educated and inspired. I can suggest no better way for their education and their inspiration than for them to realize that we who are the descendants of those who preserved Canada to the British Crown, thoroughly appreciate the responsibilities we are undertaking and are willing still further to incur responsibility in the worthy cause of our country's development. I say we are the descendants of those who preserved Canada to the British Crown. And this is true. In 1776 our French Canadian compatriots resisted the invaders, and in 1812, at Chateauguay and Lundy's Lane, men of both races co-operated towards the same good end. It is for us to prove ourselves no mean descendants of those ancestors and to leave to those who come after us a worthy and lasting heritage.
Now. I must say, I have been a little perturbed by the lateness of the hour, and
have not made the remarks I intended making. Let me say briefly that I believe in the construction of this road, and my reasons for doing so are these : The policy of the government appeals to me because it is patriotic. It will develop our country and keep our young men within our own borders, will increase our commerce and make us a nation. It is based upon a strong and earnest belief in the magnificent and certain future greatness of our country. It is practicable. It will have the further effect of strengthening confederation. As I said before, it will give a certain amount of provincial independence without having any tendency to decrease provincial inter-dependence. It will have an elevating effect on national thought and aspiration. It will promote immigration, settlement and commerce and conduce to the maintenance and furtherance of prosperity in every sphere. It is within our means. We are financially able to stand it without feeling the burden. It is thoroughly in accord with the energetic. go-ahead, optimistic spirit which has permeated this country ever since the quickening influence of Liberal rule was felt. And, when Canada becomes a. nation, a great nation, as she assuredly will, the building of this transcontinental road will be found to have been no mean factor in her growth and advancement.
On motion of Mr. Vrooman, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 12 o'clock, midnight.
